speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MORNING SITTINGS
speechtext:
I beg to move:
That on and after Tuesday, the 5th of April, 1927, until the end of the present session, the House shall meet at 11 o'clock in the morning of each sitting day, and that in addition to the usual intermission at six o'clock p.m. there shall also be an intermission every day from one to three o'clock.

speakeroldname: Hon. HUGH GUTHRIE (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: MORNING SITTINGS
speechtext: Will my right hon. friend consider the suggestion of including Saturday next in that motion?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MORNING SITTINGS
speechtext:
I thought of
holding that in reserve for the present until we see what progress we make by meeting in the morning on and after to-morrow.

subtopic: MORNING SITTINGS
speechtext:
I
would like on behalf of this part of the House to protest against this motion. Various very important committees are sitting this week right until next Friday, and many of us would like to be in the House and in the committee at the same time. This of course is impossible. It seems to me that if the work is so pressing or if we are so anxious to get away from this parliament, we are not justified, when some of us ought to be attending committees, in starting morning sitttings. For that reason I hope the House will not accept the motion.

subtopic: MORNING SITTINGS
speechtext:
I
would like to suggest to the Prime Minister that the House, instead of meeting at eleven o'clock in the morning, meet at two o'clock in the afternoon. That would be a difference
Morning Sittings

of just one hour and I think we would get through just as much business. Every possible effort is being made by members on the opposition benches to assist the government and to facilitate business. In view of that and in view of the rate at which we are getting through business, I see no reason for starting morning sessions at this particular time. Every member has a great deal of work to do other than attending the sessions of the House, and if a member has to sit in the chamber from eleven o'clock in the morning until eleven at night it is impossible for him to do justice to his work-. If the Prime Minister would take into consideration sitting at two o'clock in the afternoon, we would get through business just as well as by sitting in the morning.

subtopic: MORNING SITTINGS
speechtext:
If I had
any assurance that we would have to sit only from eleven o clock in the morning until eleven o clock at night, I would not feel so strongly against this resolution. I have a clear recollection of the last weeks of the previous session when, although we started at eleven o'clock in the morning, we sometimes had to sit in this chamber until six o'clock the following morning. If I were sure that this motion would accomplish the end which we have in view I would not oppose it. On Tuesday last we sat here from three o'clock in the afternoon until five minutes to midnight so that three hon. gentlemen could each make a speech. I do not know how those hon. gentlemen are going to get along when we apply the new rule limiting them to forty minutes. We have spent four days in discussing the Imperial conference report and we have not yet arrived at a decision. As a matter of fact there was no motion before the House to discuss except the motion to go into committee of supply.
I want to voice a protest against what appears to be unreasonable haste to wind up this session. Last year along about the 1st of July I stated in this House that I wanted to go home and many members made a good deal of fun at my expense because I used that expression. I still want to go home when the business of the House is concluded; but last year when I made that statement parliament had been sitting for about six months. This year parliament has been sitting not quite two months. One reason why I am rising in protest against this motion is because I have received numerous telegrams

from ex-service men's associations throughout Canada protesting against parliament proroguing in such a hurry and using that as an excuse for not bringing in some further legislation dealing with ex-service men's problems. Might I quote one sentence from a letter written to me recently by Mr. Lapp, superintendent of the service bureau of the Canadian Legion? He said:
The Canadian Legion of the British Empire Service League now appeals to you in the name of those who were disabled by war service and the dependents of those whose breadwinners gave their lives in the service of Canada, to remain on duty at your seat in the House of Commons of Canada for a sufficient length of time to fully consider these matters.
Many other members have been receiving similar telegrams, and I say, through you, Mr. Speaker, to the members of the Llouse and of the government that it really does not look quite right for this House to make such an effort to conclude its sittings this week. While I am very anxious to return home whenever the work of the session is completed, I do not think any hon. member can contradict me when I say that if this House prorogues this week or even by Wednesday night of the following week, the estimates mast be put through in a manner that will not permit proper consideration.

subtopic: MORNING SITTINGS
speechtext: As they always are.

speechtext:
My hon. friend says, "as
they always are." I think that is a good argument for something I have often urged in this House, and that is that the estimates be sent to a select committee for consideration, but I have never been able to get the House to adopt that suggestion. I do not suppose that I shall be able to prevent this House sitting morning, afternoon and evening, or even all night, if it wants to do it, but I simply want to make my protest as a member of the House.

subtopic: MORNING SITTINGS
speechtext:
I should not be doing what I deem to be my duty if I let this opportunity pass without a reference to one question which concerns me so far as it relates to the adjournment of the House, and that is in connection with soldier legislation. I too have received communications of various kinds, and I have felt, and I feel, that the responsibility is really upon the government for not having brought down this legislation some time ago, and they should not give as an excuse now for not bringing

it down the desire on the part of members for an early close of the session. As far as I am concerned, and I believe that a great many other hon. members feel the same way, for the fellows and the dependents of those who spent four years in the trenches in France on our behalf, we can well afford to spend one day or four days or a week or a month, if need be, to deal with any soldier legislation that may be necessary, especially in view of the shortness of this session. In that respect, therefore I protest, and I say that the government should deal with that legislation, and should not offer as an excuse for not doing so the desire for an early prorogation of the House.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MORNING SITTINGS
speechtext:
I can assure my hon. friend who has just spoken (Mr. Ladner) that the government's desire in the matter of closing at a certain date has nothing whatever to do with its decision with respect to legislation relating to the returned soldiers. The Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment (Mr. King) made a statement to the House last week in Which he gave the reasons why the government thought it inadvisable to amend that act this year beyond the one or two amendments that the minister mentioned would be brought in. I can assure my hon. friend, having regard to the number and character of the representations the minister has received, it would not be possible for the government, even if we were to be here for another month, to arrive at a decision different from that already reached in regard to those particular phases of legislation respecting returned soldiers.
I would say to my hon. friend from Macleod (Mr. Coote), who spoke of sitting late at night, that I do not think he will find anyone on this side of the House, certainly not on the government benches, who will desire any more than he does to sit up after eleven at night or midnight. The purpose of starting in the morning at eleven o'clock is if possible to get through by eleven o'clock at night, rather than running on until two or three o'clock in the morning. There does appear to be a general desire on the part of all members of the House, as far as I have been able to gather, to conclude the business by the Easter recess.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the same bill that passed the House last session but failed to pass the Senate. I think the purpose of the bill will be best explained by reading the section of the Immigration Act which it is proposed to repeal. This bill repeals section 41 of the Immigration Act, chapter 27 of the statutes of 1910, as enacted by chapter 26 of the statutes of 1919. The repealed section reads as follows:
41. Every person who by word or act in Canada seeks to overthrow by force or violence the government of or constituted law and authority in the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland or Canada, or any of the provinces of Canada, or the government of any other of His Majesty's dominions, colonies, possessions or dependencies, or advocates the assassination of any official of any of the said governments or of any foreign government, or who in Canada defends or suggests the unlawful destruction of property or by word or act creates or attempts to create any riot or public disorder in Canada or who without lawful authority assumes any powers of government in Canada or in any part thereof, or who by common repute belongs to or is suspected of belonging to any secret

Dominion Elections Act

society or organization which extorts money from or in any way attempts to control any resident of Canada, by force or by threat of bodily harm, or by blackmail, or who is a member of or affiliated with any organization entertaining or teaching disbelief in or opposition to organized government shall, for the purposes of this act, be deemed to belong to the prohibited or undesirable classes, and shall be liable to deportation in the manner provided by this act, and it shall be the duty of any officer becoming cognizant thereof and of the clerk, secretary or other official of any municipality in Canada wherein any such person may be, forthwith to send a written complaint to the minister, giving full particulars: Provided, that this section shall not apply to any person who is a British subject, either by reason of birth in Canada, or by reason of naturalization in Canada.
2.	Proof that any person belonged to or was within the description of any of the prohibited or undesirable classes within the meaning of this section at any time since the fourth day of May, one thousand nine hundred and ten, shall, for all the purposes of this act be deemed to establish prima facie that he still belongs to such prohibited or undesirable class or classes.
I might add that we are repealing section 41 because section 40 of the Immigration Act really covers all that is necessary in regard to sedition and similar offences against the state.

subtopic: VOTING BY TEACHERS AND STUDENTS

speechtext: Mr. L. P. BANCROFT (Selkirk) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 270, to amend the Dominion Elections Act (Voting by teachers and students).

subtopic: VOTING BY TEACHERS AND STUDENTS
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: VOTING BY TEACHERS AND STUDENTS
speechtext:
This bill seeks to amend paragraph (c) of section 29 of the Dominion Elections Act, which reads as follows:
Who has ordinarily resided in Canada for at least twelve months and in the electoral district wherein such person seeks to vote for at least two months immediately preceding the issue of the writ of election.
As the election writs are usually issued about two months before election day, the present act disfranchises all persons who change their places of residence during four months immediately preceding the date of an election.
School teachers begin their duties about September 1st and students in the higher institutions about October 1st.
Every federal election since 1896 has been held during the fall months. All teachers and students who, in following their respective duties, change their place of residence at the
[Mi. Forke.J
beginning of the school year, are disfranchised under the present act.
This amendment exempts teachers and students from paragraph (c) of section 29, provided that they can satisfy the registrar that they are otherwise qualified to have their names placed on the voters' list.
This amendment affects approximately 61,000 teachers and 120,000 students.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

At a conference of all parties interested, held in November of 1921, plans were made to encourage the production of the kind of hogs required to supply the British market with the best quality of bacon.
Two specific actions were agreed upon, the one interlocking with the other. The first was that market hogs should he divided into grades by Dominion government graders. The second was that where differences in price were paid for the various grades such differences should he on a minimum basis of ten per cent of the grade of "select bacon" hogs over the second grade, the "thick smooth" hogs. Thus the "thick smooth" grade became the basic grade for pricing purposes. Price differentials for the other grades were left to market conditions to establish. The policies adopted were, of course, purely experimental, no one having exact knowledge of how they would work out in practice. The understandings arrived at could not then, and cannot now, be looked upon as being permanent.
As the policy was put into operation two big factors began to emerge that complicated the carrying out of the understanding.
1.	It had been hoped that the premium of 10 per cent was to be a minimum premium and that it would he widened. But as the general quality of the hogs improved the difference in value between the "select" and the "thick smooth" grade narrowed instead of widening, owing to the better quality of the latter grade. Thus, whereas in the beginning there was a wide difference in value between the average quality of the "thick smooth" grade and the "select" which might have justified the

Questions
10 per cent premium the improvement of the "thick smooth" grade tended to narrow the difference in value to a point below 10 per cent. The premium which we believe was always recognized as an artificial and arbitrary figure adopted for the purpose of encouraging improvement became more artificial as time went on.
2.	It was found if not impossible certainly impracticable to more than partially organize the sale of hogs by farmers in such a manner as to have each farmer paid for his hogs according to quality produced. As the whole object of the policy was intended to do just that thing, the whole effort was weakened to the extent that the plan failed to accomplish its object, i.e. the payment of the individual farmer for his hogs according to grade.
Other difficulties might also be cited, such as conditions at Montreal where because very few of the hogs were used for the British trade a scheme intended to operate mainly in connection with this trade was very difficult to apply and finally when applied functions only in an arbitrary manner and is practised only by a few of the total number of operators on the Montreal markets.
But in spite of the difficulties encountered the effect has undoubtedly been to direct the efforts of all farmers in Canada to the production of a better quality of hogs. Even in the districts where hogs never have been bought on grade the hope that by the production of a better article more money might be received for it has been a factor sufficiently strong to effect improvement. By modifications which would have placed price differentials on a more natural basis and by organization in other ways most of the difficulties that were encountered probably could have been overcome. But seven or eight months ago a catastrophe overtook our industry which could not be foreseen or the full effects measured until some months after it began to operate. It is now only too plainly evident that a number of factors working together have at least for the time being ruined our trade with Great Britain. It came so suddenly and its effects were so severe that before the exporting packing plants could determine what to do it had cost the packers several millions of dollars and resulted in a most severe drain on their finances.
During the greater part of the year 1925 and 1926 the margin between the cost of feed in America to produce hogs and their selling price
has been very wide, the profit over the cost of feed running from $7 to $10 per hog on a 200-pound hog. Thus even countries that had to buy their feeds from us could easily increase production and undersell us on the British market without loss and indeed, until lately, at a fair margin of profit. The general level of prices for bacon and hogs has been for years, excepting for short periods, quite high and this has encouraged such poor countries as the Baltic states of Europe to go into the bacon business.
But the main factors that brought about the sudden collapse of the market was due to causes that originated in Britain. These were the embargoing of fresh pork imports from Holland and the weakening of the purchasing power of consumers through the effect of the great coal strike. The embargo took effect in June and in the ensuing six months Holland turning from the fresh pork trade to cured bacon sent over 60,000,000 pounds to the British market. The Baltic states increased their exports during 1926 over 1925 by about 31,000,000 pounds. This flood of European bacon coming on top of the greatly weakened buying power of the people caused prices to collapse.
In the United States and Canada, however, hog prices did not follow the course of bacon prices in England. Hog production in the United States was away below normal and prices remained far above the relative values of bacon in England. It is this situation that has been the biggest factor of all in forcing Canada out of the English market. Packers hoped for some time that it could not continue and that the high prices for hogs in the United States would increase production, but there does not now appear to be any quick solution of the problem by this means.
For a short period during the early part of 1926 bacon prices justified high prices for hogs in Canada. It had been a common experience of our packers to have prices of bacon drop below hog values and then come back again. If packers were hopeful of the situation hog prices often did not follow these drops in bacon values. So after bacon prices began to drop in 1926 hog prices carried along at an unjustifiable level, creating excessive losses which might have been minimized if the progressive nature of the decline could have been realized at the start. Finally hog prices came into line with prices in the United States. But the decline in bacon prices was so great that the loss was as serious as ever.

subtopic: TABLE OF PRICES

speechtext:
Thus the losses mounted with astonishing rapidity. Canadian packers loath to abandon their natural market held on long after they should have curtailed their shipments. Finally, their finances drained to the limit, they have had to almost abandon the British market, at least for the present. With the collapse of the British trade, packers have been forced to seek other markets, mostly in the United States. But in these markets our special type of hog receives no special consideration. Temporarily the select bacon grade when used for its special purpose, the British trade, sells at a greater loss than the other grades when they are used in the domestic trade or exported to the United States. In the domestic trade both the " select bacon " and the bacon type " thick smooth " hogs are superior to the fat type and poor quality thick smooths and the other grades. In the United States markets there are practically no differences in value for any of our grades of hogs, except of course, roughs, sows and stags.
Thus 10 per cent premium, always artificial, and even with normal conditions in the British market, becoming somewhat difficult, has now become impossible except under special conditions. Where production conditions are such that the percentage of shops, heavies, etc., allow of deductions that balance the premium the system though not justifiable might possibly be maintained were it not for the export of hogs to the United States. Buyers for these markets not being able to realize any difference in value for the different grades avoid offerings of hogs with any considerable percentage of " selects " or pay a flat price for all grades. In the district and for the shipments of hogs having the biggest percentage of " selects " the greatest difficulties have arisen. It must be recognized that where the biggest percentage of " selects " are produced the hogs as a whole are of superior quality, so that hogs in these districts really are worth more for the domestic trade. But while this is true, nevertheless it is largely a fact that the bigger the percentage of " selects " the bigger the loss to the export packer if paid for on grade. Thus in Ontario where the biggest percentage of "select" hogs are produced and which is also in close proximity to the high priced eastern United States market at Buffalo the situation has been most acute and the buying of hogs on grade has largely collapsed. The effect of flat buying in competition with a certain amount of buying on grade has been to produce unfortunate anomalies. The hogs of southwest Ontario are from the standpoint of our domestic market our poorest hogs, but are accepted on the Buffalo market at the highest price for their weights of that market. Prices for Ontario hogs are largely being based on the price of southwest Ontario hogs and " thick smooths " throughout the rest of Ontario must be merely equal to the flat price of " southwest " hogs. Thus the extra cost of selects is badly out of line with the general value of products. In the west the same condition exists but because the percentage of selects is generally low and the " outw'eight " grades comparatively high it has been possible to maintain to a great extent an artificial condition.
What then i3 to be done about it? There does not appear to be any prospect of a quick return of normal production in the United

States. There is also the possibility that the corn borer will make serious inroads in the United States corn belt within the next four or five years. The Baltic states of Europe will undoubtedly try hard to maintain their output. Poland has a population of about 28,000,000, largely agricultural, which must be reckoned with. Holland being a dairy country will continue a very considerable hog production and there is no reason to suppose that she and Denmark will not be able to maintain their present efficiency.
On the other hand sooner or later Europe and America must arrive at corresponding levels of prices for hogs and pork products. Before the war our European competitors were large producers of hogs, a great part of the products being absorbed by Germany, France and Austria. As these countries return to norma] industrial activity this condition must eventually return. After all hog production cannot exceed grain production. Formerly Denmark, Holland. Sweden and Germany purchased much of their hog feeds from Russia, Transylvania and Roumania. If any of these countries now go into hog production it reduces the grain available for export. It does not seem that Europe, unless it increases its grain production, can as a whole greatly increase its hog production. Temporarily the British market may be loaded with European product. Lastly, it does not appear that the United States will for some years at least be a natural market for our hog products. When normal production returns they will not longer want our hogs. If our hogs at any time are a menace to the United States farmers they will probably close them out by raising the tariff. We now have to pay a duty of i cent per pound on live hogs, J cent on fresh pork and 2 cents on processed pork. Thus our prices have to trail after the United States prices and if prices in the United States go down to something near their cost of production they will be below our costs which will force us to return to the British market.
So at least until the time comes when we can see the future more clearly we cannot afford to lose sight of the British market. Up to the present time almost the total burden of the struggle to maintain connection with that market has fallen on the packers. Are our farmers prepared to do something to maintain the possibilities of a return to that market? All that is required is to continue the present policy of breeding the bacon hogs. This will not cost anything as our hogs will sell at least on a par with the American hog. Suppose that at the worst the bacon bred hog brings no premium, by maintaining his blood lines the farmer will be able to return to the British market whenever the time is opportune.
It was to be expected that the artificial means set up in 1921 to accomplish a specific purpose would eventually have to be placed on a natural basis. Eventually each grade of hogs would have had to seek their real level of value whatever that level was and the plan would have had to be modified to establish natural conditions. If our normal markets had been maintained this could almost certainly have been done to considerable advantage to the industry. But it must be recognized that there is now a serious danger of making a change because the change cannot but be dras-

Questions
tie in its working. For these reasons packers have given months of consideration to the matter. It is greatly desired to retain graded buying to as great an extent as possible. But it is also recognized that it is useless under present conditions to try to set up anything even of a modified kind of artificial arrangement. Therefore, it is proposed that the grading be continued and each grade be priced according, to its value. If the bulk of our surplus hogs or their product is exported to the United States any differentials between the grades will have to depend on the values established by the domestic market. If the British trade returns the high class bacon hog will return to its own. In the meantime the bacon hog blood can be retained and increased without any sacrifice by our farmers.
The Dominion Department of Agriculture has assumed a great responsibility and work in connection with the grading of hogs, and the popularizing of the bacon hog ideal. The Provincial Departments of Agriculture have given most valuable ami able cooperation. It is fitting at this time that full credit should be given to the officers who have been engaged in the enterprise of building up the quality of our hogs. Confronted with this new situation the task of these bodies in continuing improvement work may be more difficult, but in view of the possibilities of the future the woi'k, is we believe. still of utmost importance. It is unfortunate that such changes as eventually would have been necessary in the grading plans could not have been worked out at a time when market conditions permitted a clearer view on which to formulate policy, but as we are dealing with conditions beyond our control we think it must appeal to the judgment of everyone that the only sound policy is to put into operation a system that is and will be sound under any conditions that may arise."

of this particular bill to the recommendations of that report with respect to freight rates, and to be prepared therefore to discuss the details of the bill as they arose in committee. However, I am very glad to make a general statement with regard to the matter.
As hon. members know, the royal commission appointed by the government with respect to maritime claims, comprising Sir Andrew Rae Duncan, the Hon. W. B. Wallace and Professor Cyrus MacMillan, reported upon those claims, among the most important of which is the matter of freight rates. The commission found, as set out in the preamble to the bill we are now discussing, that certain national, imperial and strategic considerations prevailed with respect to freight rates in the maritime provinces which were not present in relation to freight rates in the rest of Canada. They also found-here I am paraphrasing the report- that these considerations had been adequately met up to 1912, when increases in the freight rate structure in the maritime provinces came into effect, and that since that time these rates have been continued up to the present moment. As a matter of fact, from time to time they have been increased along with the changes made in the freight rate structure of the rest of Canada. The Duncan commission report that the recommendation which they make, to be found at page 22, is in their estimation as fair a measure of these national, imperial and strategic conditions as can be suggested and that it will have the effect particularly of restoring in the maritime provinces the parity of rates which the people there enjoyed prior to 1912. That is to say by the action proposed by the commission the relationship of freight rates in the maritime provinces to freight rates in the rest of the Dominion would be made approximately the same as it was prior to 1912.
Let me read exactly what the commission propose:
We recommend, therefore, that an immediate reduction of 20 per cent (so that 192 will become approximately 155) be made on all rates charged on traffic which both originates and terminates at stations in the Atlantic division of the Canadian National Railways (including export and import traffic, by sea, from and to that division), and that the same reduction be also applied to the Atlantic division proportion of the through rates on all traffic which originates at stations in the Atlantic division (excluding import traffic by sea), and is destined to points outside the Atlantic division.
For this purpose, we cannot regard the Atlantic division as ending at Riviere du Loup and Monk, which are its present western limits. The divisional points should, in our view, be

C.N.R.-Eastern Freight Rates
Diamond Junction and Levis, Diamond Junction being the point at which the Transcontinental railway meets the old Intercolonial railway and Levis the point to which, in 1879, the Intercolonial railway was extended.
The bill mow 'before the House meets that recommendation except in two particulars to which I shall now refer. The recommendation of the Duncan commission might be taken to imply that the reduction of 20 per cent might apply upon through rates from the maritime provinces to the United States. The legislation before the House does not provide for the reduction to apply upon the Atlantic division proportion of international rates. I shall be pleased when the bill comes 'before the committee to go into the reasons in detail as to why we could not include that in the bill. I may however state now, on the second reading that in our opinion the people of the maritime provinces would not receive any benefit from such provision had it been incorporated in the bill. I shall be glad to go into the matter more fully and give the details at greater length on the particular section of the bill when in committee.
The other omission, if omission it can be called, is that the 20 per cent reduction will not apply upon goods coming from overseas through maritime ports for distribution within the maritime provinces. That matter raised grave discriminatory questions affecting traffic coming through our ports destined to further western provinces, and the government could not see its way clear to give a 20 per cent reduction on import rates to that part of Canada which is already closest to the port through which the goods are imported. It would create a discrimination against the rest of the country, and in committee I will give the figures to indicate to our maritime friends on both sides of the House that the amount involved in the import rates is, from their point of view, very small indeed, while to make this concession would be establishing a principle which I doubt very much could be defended in this House.
The Duncan report then goes on to recommend the manner in which the relief extended should be borne. At page 22 of the report will be found the following:
The cost of this relief should be definitely borne by the Dominion government, who will make the necessary reimbursement to the Canadian National Railways through the medium of the Canadian National Railways budget, without impairing the financial results of the operation of the system.
To carry that out provision is made in the bill that the deficit on the Atlantic region which by tihe terms of the bill is extended to Diamond Junction and Levis, as recommended,

shall be kept separately and a separate item introduced in the railway budget each year to cover that deficit. Then the Duncan report goes on to say:
We are not overlooking that the other great railway system operating in the area would be entitled to equitable consideration if they find themselves prejudiced as a result of the reduction proposed.
That is a very easy way for a royal commission to escape the solution of a very difficult problem; it is very simple phraseology, but the solution is not so simple. In the first place there is not only the other great railway system to consider but in addition there are at least half a dozen other railway corporations within the area dealt with by the royal commission with respect to freight rates. I do not know that I can remember off hand their different names, but there are at least six other railway corporations which would undoubtedly be prejudiced or affected in their operations by this legislation if some machinery were not set up to take care of them.
This matter is covered in section 9, which relates not only to the other great railway corporation mentioned in the report of the commission but also to all the other railway companies operating within the area which is described as select territory for the purpose of legislation. I should say in this regard that I believe that as a result of this legislation it may be necessary for us to give consideration to the acquisition of some of these lines now being separately operated in the area from Levis and Diamond Junction to the Atlantic ocean as a part of the National system. That is a matter on which we cannot see clearly at present; it will of course require experience for us to determine the effect this legislation will have upon these various enterprises and upon the service which the people in the various districts served by these lines are receiving. That, however, is a matter not dealt with in this bill, but which I know will be raised by some of the members from the various districts concerned.
I do not know that there is anything else I need say on the second reading of the bill except to commend it to the tender mercies of the House as the first instalment-and a very large instalment-of the government's policy in implementing the recommendations of the Duncan commission.

I believe that depression was greater in extent in the maritime provinces than in any other portion of Canada, although the rest of the Dominion suffered in common from the economic developments following the cessation of hostilities.
The first manifestation of this economic development was in the federal election' of 1921, when a solid Liberal delegation was returned from Nova Scotia. I may say in passing that I do not propose to treat this matter from 'the standpoint of party politics, although from statements made by the Prime Minister announcing this legislation and from the action of a small body of Liberal politicians in New Brunswick it may be necessary to revert briefly to the political aspect. As .1 say, the economic depression in the maritime provinces made itself manifest in the result of the general election in 1921, when the province of Nova Scotia sent a solid delegation of sixteen members to support the present Prime Minister; when the province of Prince Edward Island sent a solid delegation of four members to sit behind the Prime Minister and when the province of New Brunswick practically divided. It is my considered judgment that had that large delegation, knowing the economic conditions which obtained in the maritime provinces at that time, pressed upon the government of the day those considerations which were subsequently brought to their attention by gentlemen representing the maritime provinces from this side of the House, it would not have been necessary to wait five years for the legislation brought down to-day, and we could have avoided five years of depression with the consequent loss of earning power, prosperity and economic manhood and womanhood. Because of the failure of those gentlemen representing the maritime provinces in the fourteenth parliament of this country, grave dissatisfaction arose in that pant of Canada. The first result of that dissatisfaction was shown in the Halifax by-election, after which came the Kent by-election and finally the general elections of 1925. I claim, Sir, that this legislation brought down to-day is the direct result of the action of the people of those provinces in the year 1925. Be that as it may, I think history will accord to those gentlemen who took up the flaming torch of maritime rights
during those years the credit which is their due, notwithstanding what may have been said here, there, or elsewhere.
The greatest need of the maritime provinces undoubtedly is in connection with this very question of transportation; on that I think we all agree. I think I can safely say that there is a certain degree of satisfaction felt by all parties representing those provinces in the bill immediately under discussion, and I say that as fairly as I possibly can. I must also say, however, that the people down there will find themselves very much disallusioned when they learn what has been authoritatively stated by the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) to-day, that these rates do not apply to international shipments. Speaking for the producers of New Brunswick, I can say that by far the greater volume of the tonnage shipped over our railways is international tonnage, consisting of pulp, pulp-wood, lumber and the products of our fields, particularly potatoes. I do not refer especially to fish because we do not export so much of that commodity from the province of New Brunswick; that is a matter more particularly affecting Nova Scotia. Since that occasion I have not had the privilege of being down in the maritime provinces, consequently I cannot say whether they have improved their economic condition since then. No doubt it probably has improved to seme small extent, if not to the extent that they would like.
This proposed legislation arises out of the report of the royal commission that was appointed last year to inquire into the question of the alleged maritime claims. The representatives of the maritimes who have presented their claims have stated on many occasions that the people of the maritimes were under a handicap or disability because of the fact that they had entered into confederation. As far as the report of the commission is concerned, it rejects that contention altogether. The commissioners state emphatically in their report that in their viewpoint that claim cannot be substantiated. Let me quote from the introduction to the report:
The outstanding fact, it seems to us, is that the maritime provinces have not prospered and developed, either in population, or in commercial, industrial and rural enterprise, as fully as other portions of Canada. We are unable to take the view that confederation, is, of itself, responsible for this fact. The trend and nature of economic development generally throughout the last sixty years has made !within the maritimes changes in the structure of business and employment which are unrelated to confederation, and which would have taken place whether or not the maritime provinces had been independent units outside of Confederation. Even within confederation there has been such a measure of responsibility resting on each
province for its own development that much at least of what has happened within the Maritime provinces must be related to their responsibility and not to the responsibility of the Dominion.
That is a very emphatic statement, Mr. Speaker, and it comes from the commission itself. They state that much responsibility lies within the maritime provinces themselves, that they themselves are largely responsible for the condition the}' are in to-day, and not the Dominion as a whole.
There is another quotation I wish to make from the report, and this is my last, dealing with the question of a general stocktaking in Canada, a review of the situation throughout the length and breadth of the country in order to see how the component parts of the confederation are progressing and ascertain their needs, if needs they have. On page 1 of the introduction to the report the commissioners state:
But reasonable balance is within accomplishment if there be periodic stocktaking. We venture to regard the present occasion as such a period of stocktaking, so that in the future progress of the common great enterprise the prospects of the maritime provinces may be brought into line with the prospects of other parts of Canada and the prospects of the Dominion as a whole.
I think every hon. member of this House will accord support to that statement. Realizing as we do how far-flung this country is, and its great diversity of interests, it is only reasonable to expect that once in a while a general stocktaking of the situation within Canada should be had in order to see how the component parts are progressing.
Coming to the proposed legislation, we find set out in the preamble, as the minister has already stated, certain claims. In the first place, the Intercolonial railway was built as part of the confederation pact. There is no question about that; no one denies it. The next claim is that this railway was built primarily for national and imperial reasons, together with the object of giving the manufacturers and traders of the maritime provinces a larger market in the central and western provinces of Canada. It is quite true that this railway was built primarily because of confederation. It is true also that the route it follows is a much longer route than probably would have been chosen if it had not been that the builders had to take into consideration national and imperial needs and the necessity for an outlet and inlet on the Atlantic seaboard.
But there is another question that is also important in connection with this railway. It is claimed that because of the course followed, the curvatures and the grades are not such

as will allow the railway to be operated with efficiency. That is a very important consideration which the proposed legislation does not take into account. This legislation does not make any provision for the elimination of these sharp curvatures and heavy grades, and consequently we are not going to have a railway which can be operated efficiently. This point should not be lost sight of in dealing with this important matter. But I will come back to that a little later.
It is claimed that the rates in the maritime provinces have increased to a greater extent than they have in other parts of Canada. That in a measure is true. We must remember that while there was an increase in certain classes of rates in 1912, there was also an increase in local rates in 1016, I believe, and I wish to deal with that a little more fully so that we may have these rates properly before us. I am going to take the time of the House for a few minutes to follow the rate structure from the earliest time of which we have any records down to the present, so that the House may understand the situation.
Following the opening of the all-rail route between Montreal and St. John, New Brunswick, the through rates from the maritimes to points west were made up of arbitraries over the Montreal rate. The earliest record is the tariff of 1891-1894, showing an arbitrary of 30 cents added to the Montreal rate to make the through rate to and from St. John. The record is not clear 'between 1894 and 1900, but during this period the arbitrary was reduced from 30 to 20 cents, and the 20 cent rate was continued until 1916, when in the eastern rate case it was raised to 24 cents.

Now, the other day I noticed in the Citizen a statement by a Mr. Cornell who, I understand, appeared before the Duncan commission on behalf of the maritime provinces in regard to freight rates. In the Ottawa Citizen of March 24, 1927, appeared the following:
Ottawa, March 23.-"The implementing of the Duncan report with regard to transportation costs and facilities will undoubtedly be a long step toward reinstating a proper basis of transportation costs and services in the Maritimes," says a statement issued here to-day by F. C. Cornell, K.C., who presented the case for the maritime governments with regard to freight rates before the Duncan commission.
Mr. Cornell estimated that $5,000,000 would be a conservative estimate of the amount involved in the rate reductions.
It is quite true, probably, that Mr. Cornell thought the Duncan report would be implemented in full, which would naturally take into consideration the traffic that my hon. friend who preceded me dealt with. However, it will be interesting to listen to the Minister of Railways in committee and discover what his estimate is of the cost to the taxpayers of Canada. It is presumed that this bonusing of rates to the extent of 20 per cent is going to make a good deal of difference to the people of the maritime provinces. In some particulars it may assist them somewhat, but I am very doubtful whether on the whole it will create the measure of prosperity which we should all like to see in the maritime provinces in the near future.
Last year, representing the constituency of Shelburne-Yarmouth in this House, was a gentleman who, fortunately or unfortunately for himself, is now in another chamber. I wish to quote a brief paragraph from a speech he made last session on this maritime question. The remarks I am about to read, from revised Hansard of 1926, page .3436, refer to the freight rate on fish, and I hope hon. members will follow me in this quotation, wh^ph has an important bearing if the contentions therein set out are correct. The member in question had this to say:
Now as to fish. Can we, through the process of cheapening the freight rates, ever find a. sufficiently large market in central Canada for1 our fish so as to enable us to build up a great fish industry in the province of Nova Scotia? Hon. gentlemen must take this fact into account:
the man who catches the fish gets from one to two cents a pound for it. Afterwards there is a shrinkage in the fish to the extent, perhaps, of forty or fifty per cent. Finally it is sold up here for twenty-five cents a pound, and the freight amounts to $1.80 per hundred pounds. You can see from these figures where you are going to get in, undertaking to create a big demand for fish in the central provinces through the process of cheapening the freight rates. If we are ever to have a market established here for our fish there must be a lessening of the spread between the price as paid to the producer and what the consumer has to pay for his fish.
I do not know whether the gentleman just quoted was correct in his statement that the fishermen receive from one to two cents per pound for their fish. Probably the figures he gives in regard to freight rates are absolutely correct. Nor am I sure whether that same fish is sold at twenty-five cents per pound in this part of the country. But when you take into consideration the fact that, according to this gentleman's statement, it costs only $1.80 per 100 pounds to transport fish from the maritime provinces into central Canada, it will be realized that a 20 per reduction in freight rates will not amount to very much so far as the fishermen are concerned. I do not think they will benefit to any great extent. Furthermore, I doubt whether the consumer, so far as any of these rates go, will receive any great benefit from the present proposal. It is quite probable that before this bill passes the House we shall hear members referring to special legislation that has been adopted in the matter of freight rates in regard to the grain growers of western Canada. It would be only natural to expect, after the statements I have made, someone to get up and say "You in western Canada have received special legislation, and it is due to the maritime provinces that legislation of a similar character be enacted in their interests." This will help us to judge the two methods of approach to an important question. Before the railway committee last week one of the officials of the railways made the statement that the Crowsnest rates were a losing proposition for the railways in the west. Up until the year 1896, I believe, railway companies used to come to the government of Canada and secure subsidies by way of land and money grants, but the people were getting pretty well tired of that sort of thing. Finally, when the Laurier government came into power in 1896, the Canadian Pacific Railway approached the government for assistance in the construction of what is known as the Crows-nest pass railway. True, the government felt that in view of public opinion they could not give a straight money grant or subsidy, but they found ways and means of meeting the difficulty. There were certain rates in effect at that particular time on the main line of the Canadian Pacific Railway and the government of the day gave a cash grant of so much per mile in consideration of an agreement entered into by the Canadian Pacific Railway that the rates should never be higher than they were then. It cost this country $3,400,000 to implement that agreement with the Canadian Pacific, and since that time grain rates in western Canada have been below that level for many years. Hon. members, more particularly those who were in this House some years ago, will recall the fact that the western rates were finally suspended, coming into effect again in part in 1922, and partly again at a later date.
Now, the claim has been made that these Crowsnest rates are a losing proposition for the railways, and in that regard I want to place on Hansard, for the information of hon. members, certain evidence bearing on the subject. Now, Mr. Speaker, there is quite a difference between these two classes of legislation. In the legislation now before us it is proposed to grant a subsidy to certain classes of traffic in the maritime provinces, while the Crows-nest rates on grain are a paying proposition. It is true that there is a maximum above which the railways are not supposed to charge, but notwithstanding what the railways and those who apologize for the railways have said, the evidence I have just read is ample proof that the Crowsnest rates are paying and at least the Canadian lines of our Canadian railways earn the greater bulk of their profits through the hauling of grain from western Canada, It is quite true that during the six months' period indicated in the statement I have read there is quite a movement of other goods, but that is by virtue of the fact that the harvest is imminent in western Canada. The grain movement causes these other movement of goods, and hon. members will recognize at once the value of the grain grower in western Canada to the total business of this country.
I do not think this particular legislation will be of very great help to the maritime provinces, because it does not touch any of the basic economic problems which they have to face. Unless you deal with those problems all that can be said of this legislation is that it is simply a handout for the time being. It is very similar to a man who comes to vour back door out of work and hungry; you give him a handout by way of some food or a little money but that does not solve his problem^ of being out of work and unable to earn a living.

If you cannot secure reasonable lines of credit, or if you have to submit your case to the head office in either Montreal or Toronto, probably a thousand miles away, you are not going to receive the same consideration as you would if there was a head office in the locality or a different banking system. It is reasonably safe to say that the banking system of the United States, while it is true there have been many casualties, has been largely responsible for the splendid development of that country, because the people who control those different banks, localized as they are, are interested in the development of the locality and consequently those parts of the United States flourished to a greater extent than they would have done under our banking system. I merely throw out as a suggestion that this matter might be given some serious consideration. I know hon. members to my right will pooh-pooh the idea that there is any connection between banking credit and success in business. There is a very close connection. Without reasonable banking credit you can never hope to make any business a success.
I regret that the government has introduced this legislation in this manner. I wish to see the maritimes prosper; I would1 like to see this House do everything legitimate to allow them to prosper, but I think the best way to give them an opportunity to prosper is to give them an opportunity to help themselves. I am not of opinion that handing out bonuses or subsidies of this description is in the interest of the people to whom they are handed out. There are many things that could be done to assist the maritime provinces. I am not satisfied that the commission made a proper economic study of the situation. If they had done so, I think their report would not be as it is to-day, because in my judgment, at any rate as far as the report indicates, they did not begin to touch the basic economic factors, and until you remedy the conditions that attach to those economic factors, there can be no prosperity in the maritime provinces. Handing out bonuses may help them for a time, but it will be only for a time and they will be back here asking for something else.

To a large extent the Duncan report supports the requests that were made at that time, in 1920. Not a word was said, no reply even was given to the representations then made by the three governments of the maritime provinces, and in 1921, again to keep the record straight, the same representations were made, and when the elections came on in that year the representative of the province of New Brunswick in the government of Canada, being then the Minister of Customs in that government, sat in council, and there was staring him in the face the request of the maritime provinces to protect our Canadian ports, and to prevent the export of wheat through American ports. He sat there when an order in council was passed by which he consented that $1,450,000 should be voted for the maintenance, upkeep and repair of the docks in the port of Portland, against the claims of the city of St. John, New Brunswick. That is the record, Mr. Speaker. I do not wish to go any further into that. I merely mention it because I want to keep the record straight, and I hope the next time my hon. friend speaks of maritime rights he will leave the political issue out of it.
I do not intend to go to any extent into the details of the argument which have been presented. I am much surprised that my hon. friend from Acadia (Mr. Gardiner) is not more sympathetic, coming from a place of that name, when he knows that in old Acadia, the oldest colony in Canada to-day, there is
[Mr. Veniot.J
a feeling in favour of what we call fair play, and I want to say to him that he has a misconception of the reasons why the maritime provinces are asking for this measure of justice. I want it to be distinctly understood -and I believe it is understood, and it will not be necessary for me to say it-that the maritime provinces are not before the House of Commons as suppliants for favours. We are here standing on the pact of confederation, and when my hon. friend from Acadia makes a comparison between this legislation and the legislation that brought about the Crowsnest pass rates, it is apparent he never lias studied history. If he had studied the history of confederation he would have found that there was a pact between the fathers of confederation and old Canada, at that time Ontario and Quebec, that if we would consent to come into confederation they on theiir part would do so-and-so in order to help us out 'commercially, economically as they said, and otherwise, and when they laid the proposition before the maritime provinces those provinces were very prosperous. In 1867 Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island were prosperous, and showed greater prosperity than the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. While I am a strong and firm believer in confederation, while to-day I would not change my allegiance so far as confederation is concerned, I want it to be understood that I come down from a family that fought confederation from the beginning almost until the death of the parent that brought me into this world. I later on understood what confederation would mean, not only to Canada but to British connection on the North American continent, and for that I stood and for that I stand to-day. I want the rest of Canada to understand that when Nova Scotia and New Brunswick came into confederation in 1867, drawn into it almost against their will, when they were called upon to make the sacrifice they did it on account of a deep rooted sense of loyalty to the British Empire. and a desire to maintain British supremacy in this half of the North American continent.
When the proposition was placed before the maritioTes to go into confederation, the question of constructing a national railway came up, and it was pointed out that the Intercolonial railway could in five years become a paying proposition, but not if we were forced to build it, or to consent to its construction, along or.in the direction laid down. By whom? Not by Canada of that day, Ontario and Quebec, but as a result of representations made from Great Britain

through the admiralty to our Canadian authorities, that to build a road along the line originally proposed would endanger British connection, because at any time an unfriendly nation-although at that time the nation to the south was not unfriendly-might take charge of the railroad and prevent the transportation of troops and prevent the ports of Halifax and St. John, from being used in aid of 'Great Britain should war break out. The railroad was distinctly promised to the people of the maritime provinces and there is no gainsaying the fact. People may say "You cannot find it in the law". It is true it is not enacted in the law, but Canada can depend upon the honour of its public men such as Sir John A. Macdonald, or Sir George Etienne Cartier, or the Hon. George Brown. We in the maritime provinces depended on their word of honour, and I desire to say to this House that the word of honour of these men, in so far as it touched or related to the Intercolonial railway, was kept until 1912.
For forty long years the Intercolonial railway was administered and operated in accordance with the promise given to us when we entered confederation. The freight rates at that time were arbitrary and preferential and so arranged as to bring back, or help to bring back, to the maritimes something in return for the sacrifices they made when in the name of loyalty they came into confederation. Up to 1912 the maritimes enjoyed those rates, and I want to correct my hon. friend. Sir Andrew Duncan need not say it to convince me of the truth of the statement; I knew it before Sir Andrew came to this country. The Intercolonial was completed in 1876, and it would appear from the evidence we have that from that time till 1912 the interests of the maritime provinces were fairly well guarded, the freight rates structure being such as to take into account the requirements of their traffic.
Let me once more keep the record straight. In 1912 an act was introduced into this House of Commons sanctioning the increase of freight * rates on the old Intercolonial, and my hon. friend from York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson), who has tried to inject a tinge of politics into this matter, might go back to that record and ask who was in power at that time. It was not the Liberal party that was in poweT in 1912. I want to draw the attention of the House, especially the attention of my friends in the far-off corner, to the fact that in 1912, before we undertook to increase the freight rates on the Intercolonial and make them equal to the freight rates in Upper Canada, the Intercolonial had a surplus of $1,000,000. While I am
on the question of surpluses and deficits, let me say to this House that in all the forty years of operation of the Intercolonial the operating losses were a little over $9,000,000, while during the same period the surpluses amounted to $1,666,000. All right. Let me go a little further for the sake of those who have not read the history of the maritime provinces. When New Brunswick and Nova Scotia came into confederation we had a railway from St. John to Shediac, and another, the old eastern section, from Halifax down to New Glasgow. Each of those railways was being operated by the provincial governments and making money. We handed them over as a part of the Intercolonial to the government of the day as one of the terms of the confederation bargain. We had undertaken to continue the road from Truro to St. John, and thence to the American border in order that we might get our natural and manufactured products into t-he New' England states. What happened? The Imperial government in conjunction with the government of Canada, then Ontario and Quebec, forbade us to proceed with our undertaking for fear of international complications that might arise, and we were forced to accept this road along the north shore, 250 miles more in length than it otherwise would have been, to reach the seaports Of the maritimes. It is for these reasons that to-day we are asking that faith be kept with us in regard to the Intercolonial railway.
Now, some of my hon. friends in discussing this matter tried to be fair, I suppose, but

they were not fair. This may be because they do not entirely understand the situation. I am not going to undertake to meet the hon. gentleman from Acadia on all the freight rate comparisons he made between different sections of the west and the east. Allow me to say, though, to him that we do not regret any transportation advantage now enjoyed by the western provinces. Indeed, we are prepared to continue it because we are patriotic enough to pay our share, to help with our little mite in making the west more prosperous, even if we have to go down deep into our pockets to do so. My western friends will always find the maritimes ready to fight side by side with them for what they can convince us to be right; and what we are prepared to do for them in the way of fair play we expect they will do for us in so far as the maritimes are concerned.

Now some hon. members who have been listening to me may have some doubts as to the justice of our claim for what is ours by right under the pact of confederation. For the sake of these hon. gentlemen let me quote the observations of one of our great statesmen of that generation with reference to the Intercolonial railway. Speaking at Halifax on September 12, 1864, Sir John A. Macdonald said:
I do not hesitate to say that, with respect to the Intercolonial railway, it is understood by the people of Canada-

That is, Quebec and Ontario.
-that it can only be built as a means of political union for the colonies. It cannot be denied that the railway as a commercial enterprise would be of comparatively little commercial advantage to the people of Canada.
Then Ontario and Quebec.
While we have the St. Lawrence in summer, and the American ports in time of peace, we have all that is requisite for our purpose. We recognize, however, the fact that peace may not always exist, and that we must have some other means of outlet if we do not wish to be cut off from the ocean for months in the year. We wish to have greater security-to know that we can have assistance readily in the hour of danger. In the case of union, this railway must be a national work, and Canada will cheerfully contribute to the utmost extent to make that important link without which no political connection can be complete in Canada.
There Sir John A. Macdonald recognized this as a national enterprise and he was fully cognizant that the honour of Canada

that is, Quebec and Ontario-was at stake. If the Intercolonial had been built as a commercial enterprise and the maritime provinces had entered confederation distinctly on the understanding that the road would be built only as a commercial railway, then we of the maritimes to-day would be ready, to use a common expression, to take our medicine with the rest of the country. But that is not the case; we came into confederation on certain definite and well understood conditions. Just as Ontario and Quebec, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and British Columbia all entered confederation in their respective days on condition that certain things would be done, so the maritime provinces joined the union fully believing that the pact would be lived up to so far -as what was promised them. The government of this country is therefore in duty bound to adhere to the conditions of confederation, no matter what sacrifice this may mean to the treasury of the Dominion. That is the stand we take today, and it is the stand which I know every honest man in this House and in the country, every man who believes in British fair play, every man who believes that our public honour should be vindicated, will defend. Although we may not always see eye to eye with one another in our political transactions, although we may not all play the political game on the same side, the time, I firmly believe, has come when the people in this Dominion, of all shades of political opinion, are broad enough in mind and spirit to see that after sixty years of confederation the maritime provinces shall receive their due. I have faith enough in the broadmindedness and the sense
of justice of Canadians to believe that there will be a general desire in this country to endorse such legislation as is necessary to implement the confederation agreement so far as the maritime provinces are concerned.
The Intercolonial was taken away from the maritimes in 1912 for no satisfactory reason whatever; it was not necessary to increase freight rates in order to make it self-sustaining.
I therefore appeal with confidence to hon. members in all parts of the House to restore to us in that part of the Dominion that which rightfully belongs to us, and which will put us in a happier position, where we can feel that we are not abandoned by the rest of Canada. I know that when justice is done the maritime provinces by this Dominion there will be a widespread spirit of contentment in those provinces and a greater degree of happiness than at present exists. There never has been any fear on the part of the people of the maritime provinces that that section of the Dominion would ever become disloyal, either to Canada or to the British Empire at large. The people of the maritimes, in this sixtieth anniversary of confederation, are just as true to the Dominion as they have been at any time in its history, and if such calamity as occurred in 1914 should take place again I can assure the House that the maritime provinces will once again rally to the defence of British institutions. All we ask now is that we be given that modicum of fair play to which we are convinced we are entitled.

The legislation to equalize freight rates was enacted, in my opinion, to find an excuse for robbing western Canada of statutory protection against the skyrocketing of freight rates, and it has lain dormant here for two years, during which time a part of the crop has been hauled out, not on Crowsnest rates, but at a higher rate not regulated- at all by the Crowsnest pass agreement. Now added to that, we have to bear one-fifth of the rate charged in a part of Canada which lies by the sea, and which, from an export country like Canada, should find a market for its products overseas. The maritimes also have the advantage of having a line of boats running below cost to their most prolific market, under the West India agreement, and the deficit on that service will have to be met every year by the country at large. The west has an average rail haul of 1,800 miles to reach tidewater, on which it is charged from 15 to 20 per cent more than any other part of the Dominion.
Again, I would quote an editorial from the Free Press which has gone out throughout western Canada, -and I hope the west is taking particular notice of this. The Free Press of Winnipeg asks: "If this ds the case, why should -the west have to pay rates averaging 15 to 20 per cent higher than the tariff in eastern Canada? Have we been paying more because the railways were able to gat away with it? Why should the rates foe higher in the west especially when it has been shown that the cost of operation on the prairies is lower than anywhere else in Canada." This is something for the west to think about.



C.N.R.-Eastern Freight Rates
The admission made by Mr. Watson before the railway commission that a special privilege is given to the manufacturers on their products going to western Canada which somebody else has to pay for was quoted by my hon. friend from Acadia this afternoon. That admission clarifies the situation somewhat. But that is not all the privilege these manufacturers receive at the people's expense. For instance, the rates from Ontario and Quebec to the maritime provinces or to maritime ports are to-day 18 cents per hundredweight less than from the maritimes to Quebec and Ontario points; the traffic expert of the three prairie provinces is my authority for that statement. I want to tell this House that while the Crowsnest pass agreement did prevent to some extent the skyrocketing of freight rates in western Canada, the manufacturers in this privileged area in Ontario and Quebec enjoy a rate both ways that does not begin to cover the cost of the service.
Another feature of the policy of the government is this, that while ignoring their own measure to equalize freight rates over this Dominion, they also ignore the fact that the present rate structure to and from the maritimes is based on the short straight haul of the Canadian Pacific railway, and not as put forward by the maritime righters on the Canadian National railway, our old Intercolonial, which was constructed over a route 250 miles longer than it should have been. Those 250 miles which were built, as they say, for strategic purposes, are surely a benefit to those provinces since the railway rate is based on the short haul, and it has been responsible for a part of the deficit which the country has had to meet nearly every year. This has been practically a subsidy to those provinces ever since confederation. The 20 per cent proposed in this bill is an extra subsidy to be paid to cheapen the transportation of products of the maritimes going west. It is not meant to widen the markets of the maritimes for their products by hauling them further west, but is simply to be a charge on the taxpayer presented by way of a bill each year by the railway companies to parliament for the haulage of freight over this division. No one knows what it will cost. If it proves successful in improving conditions it will be to that extent each year an increasing burden on the rest of the Dominion. I say it is unfair because the present rate is based upon the Canadian Pacific railway straight haul, and not on the National Transcontinental. No one who has advocated maritime rights in this House during the last two or three years has ever once asserted that any pledge was given to these provinces at the

time of confederation regarding this matter: that, after providing means by which their produce could be marketed in the Dominion, [DOT]the Dominion was to pay any part of the haulage cost. No pledge was given regarding freight rates, and no one expected that part of the freight rate would ever have to be paid for them; in fact the Duncan report failed to establish the fact that any of the present trouble was due to any promises or pledges given at confederation. The rates in the maritime provinces have never been higher than the rates in the provinces of Quebec and Ontario, and anyone using the Crows-pest pass agreement as an argument for this subsidy must not forget that the Crowsnest pass rates were higher than in any other part of Canada on a given commodity over a given distance.
But let us look at this matter from another angle. When the maritime provinces, by agitation and threats of secession, can obtain a free gift of one-fifth of its rail rates, which are lower now by fifteen to twenty per cent than in some other parts of the Dominion, is it not natural that western Canada may ask herself if she is not paying too high a price to remain in confederation, and there will be more excuse for complaint than has ever been in the maritime provinces. Further than that, what will the industrial areas of Ontario and Quebec care how much they pay in taxes to meet their subsidy each year, as long as they can pass it on in the price of the goods they manufacture doiwn here, and compel us to buy at their own price? By this measure I say the government is simply increasing the dose of the dope that has already reduced the country to a state of helplessness. This legislation is only a short cut-out for the time, and I can but classify it as shortsighted, unfair, vicious and unstatesmanlike. I am in sympathy with the maritime provinces as they are, but I want to meet conditions as they exist and go to the root of the evil now.

Limited, St. John, N.B., .president of the St. John Board of Trade. Surely this man knows what he is talking about. I will quote one or two paragraphs from this pamphlet. He says:
Turning to industry; the story of the maritime provinces under this head since confederation is a long series of tragedies. Some would-be comforters have tried to convince us, without knowledge of the facts, that the hard times in the maritimes were but the result of post-war depression that was common to all sections; but this industrial record belies them. You will find splendid industrial plants in many places in the maritimes standing gaunt and empty, or the stark ruins of once thriving industries staring mutely in a setting of tumbling cottages, once happy homes, their owners forced to go to New England for a livelihood. Not a few of these have been bought out, closed down, and dismantled by central Canadian competitors.
Then after describing how industry under the system of protection has been closed out to the maritime provinces by combines located in this central area, he says that the customs tariff and the law of trade restriction reduced the people to the state of slavery.

In doing that it has to compete with the cheap labour of Asia and certain countries of Europe where men are paid a few copecks a day. It is unreasonable to compare the wheat pool with combines that are organized by the politicians of this country. The customs and tariff acts to-day are so administered as to give not only the manufacturers but the distributors the pricefixing power that they desire. Mr. Simms has well pointed this out in the paragraph which I have read from his address. Surely my friends from the maritimes are bound to take note of this fact.
Now, the government instead of meeting the real cause of trade stagnation in the maritimes, which is practically the protective tariff, have withheld the maritime report from this House for discussion, and in this piecemeal fashion seek still to aid the same combines which with this price-fixing power have despoiled the maritimes and now seek to clean up the whole Dominion. I say that deliberately. When the burdens of the maritimes are placed on the taxpayers of the whole country, it is simply a declaration on the part of the government that they are not willing to meet the real cause of the evil- the price-fixing power which they have given to these combines. Is it any wonder that maritime freight rates are high? Is it any wonder that freight rates are high throughout the Dominion? It is simply because the railway workers, to some extent, have been able to organize and demand a wage rate somewhat commensurate with the high cost of living caused by these combines. Mr. Speaker, my remarks on the second reading of this bill will be very brief. I realize the desire on the part of every member to finish this session at the earliest possible moment, and I would not say anything on the bill at all if I did not deem it my duty to do so. Thus far in the debate no one on either side of the House has given expression to a very wide spread sentiment existing in the maritime provinces at the present time, namely, a sentiment of appreciation of the efforts of the government in introducing this and other measures for the benefit of the maritime provinces. I was very much surprised this afternoon to hear the partisan speech of the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson), and I should like to remind the House that in his remarks he did not in any way represent the true sentiment, either Liberal or Conservative, of the maritime provinces. I can assure hon. members that the feeling of the people of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island is one of appreciation of the government's activities at the present time.
I do not propose to go very fully into the merits of the bill before the House. The bill carries out one of the findings of the commission which was presided over by Sir Andrew Duncan. It has the weight of the findings of a non-partisan, independent and judicial inquiry presided over by a brilliant Englishman, Which of itself, in my opinion, creates the presumption that these
