findings are sound and should be implemented by legidation.
I want to congratulate the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston), the Postmaster General (Mr. Veniot), the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) and particularly the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) upon the statesmanlike way in which this whole question of maritime rights has been handled. If we look back on the agitation which has been made for a recognition of maritime claims I think it will be agreed that there is not a man in this House, indeed there is not a person in the maritime provinces, who will not now say that the proper step to have taken was precisely the step that was taken, namely, the appointment of an independent commission of inquiry. It will be recalled that, during the course of the agitation for maritime rights, various views were put forward by various persons in the maritime provinces as to what should and what should not be done in that part of Canada. The Conservative party conducted the agitation for some years with great political success. They suggested a number of remedies of various sorts. Some of these suggestions have been condemned by the Duncan commission while others have been partially adopted. The course of the Conservative party in the province of Nova Scotia in the matter of maritime claims has been a tortuous one. In the year 1923 they started by advocating secession of the province. A little later they branched off to secession of the Intercolonial railway; and in the array of remedies which they advocated one was always in the forefront, namely, the restoration of the integrity of the Intercolonial railway. No one believes to-day that the integrity of the Intercolonial railwaj'- should be restored, that is to say, that the Intercolonial should be withdrawn from the Canadian National system. As a matter of fact the Duncan commission specifically finds against anything of that sort being done. I say, therefore, that the Prime Minister took the proper course when he decided, prior to the session of 1926, upon the appointment of a non-partisan commission of inquiry. It will be remembered that in the session of 1926 the government was bitterly assailed by the members from Nova Scotia on the Conservative side because of the appointment of that commission. It is quite interesting at this time to find the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) attempting, as he did this afternoon, to claim for the Conservative party credit for what has been accomplished. It is interesting to refer to Hansard of last year to see what stand was taken then by hon. members on
the Conservative side of the House in relation to the appointment of this commission. My predecessor in the representation of Hants-Kings cun page 969, said this:

To begin with, in regard to the question of freight rates, the Duncan commission has recommended three times as much in the way of benefits to the maritime provinces in this direction than the Conservative party ever advocated. The whole remedy as prescribed by the Conservatives of Nova Scotia for the conditions in those provinces consisted in the reduction of freight rates on certain traffic originating in the maritime provinces and terminating in central Canada.

: That was the sum total of their proposal, You may scan their platform from beginning to end and you will not see any evidence of its having occurred to them that there was anything wrong with other freight rates than those on traffic originating in the east and terminating in central Canada. The Duncan report, on the other hand, properly recognizes the importance to the maritime provinces of local traffic and of the export trade. I was very much interested this afternoon to hear, from the lips of the hon. member for York-Sunbury, admissions which he never would have made in 1911, for instance, the admission that maritime produce is rushing by carloads from New Brunswick into the United' States. In my own constituency, I know, the most important feature of the Duncan report, so far as freight rates are concerned, has to do with the export rates. In my constituency we grow a great many apples. Of this commodity we export more from that constituency, than is shipped from any other part of Canada. Some time ago I had occasion to look into the figures to see -where these apples went and I found, taking the last five years, that of every 100 barrels of apples packed and shipped in Nova Scotia only seven went to the central provinces, while nine were sold in the maritime provinces and no fewer than eighty-four were sold abroad, most of them in the English market. Take potatoes, of which we raise large quantities:	ninety-nine per cent of our
potatoes go to the United States, Cuba and the West Indies. In the county of Hants we have large deposits of gypsum, more probably than in all the rest of Canada put together. East year our output was 600,000 tons, practically all of which went to the New England States and to New York. Take, again, evaporated apples. We sent 300,000 barrels of apples to the evaporators in 1925. The finished product went largely to Germany and the Netherlands. Practically all of it was marketed abroad. And a great many of our other farm products such as turnips and strawberries, to mention a few, go to the New England states; others produced in the constituency, and which I cannot recall at the moment, find their markets abroad. It is therefore of the utmost importance to people in. that part of Nova Scotia that the export rates should be lowered. From the map it may be thought that, being on the sea, we have no export rates to pay. This is not so. In the matter of apples, for instance, the rate from the town of Berwick in the county of Kings, which is a large shipping point, to Halifax was seventeen cents per barrel in 1915; it is now thirty-four and a half cents. The 
shippers consider that the rates on apples form an onerous burden which is not justified by the circumstances, and they are looking with great interest to the action of the government with respect to export rates.
With regard to the course this debate took this afternoon, I do not intend to pursue the lines of inquiry which were then started, but I agree with a great deal of what has been said by the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Gardiner) and1 by the hon. member for Rosetown (Mr. Evans). From the best consideration I can give the economic history of the province of Nova Scotia I believe that the question of tariffs is more important than that of freight rates, and that the greatest injury to that province has been done by the protective policy of Canada. I am not here to enter into a discussion of protection versus free trade, but I believe that the population figures, the figures relating to industry, and the facts which are apparent from an examination of the whole countryside show that the decline has been rapid in the province of Nova Scotia since and because of the protective tariff of 1879 and those Which have followed. I am fully aware that certain industries in Nova Scotia may benefit from a. protective tariff, such as the steel industry and possibly the coal industry, but nothing is more useless and nothing is more absurd than for hon. gentlemen to get up in this House and advocate a duty of SI or $2 or $3 on coal, because at present it is not at all practicable.

With regard to the question of my hon. friend I will say that under the democratic tariff the duty on fish was lowered for some years, and perhaps some kinds of fish were allowed to enter the United States free. At any rate, that does not in any way detract from the argument I have been making.	_
1 have referred to the Canadian and American tariffs, and next in importance to those have been the high freight rates, the gradual rise of freight rates on the Intercolonial railway. The historical course of events was set out very well this afternoon, and I do not need to repeat very much of it. The Intercolonial railway was built not as a commercial enterprise but as a public work, a national undertaking; its route was chosen not from commercial considerations but because of strategic considerations, and the understanding was that it was to be a great highway of traffic between the maritime provinces and the central parts of Canada. From its completion in 1876 until 1912 the understandings entered into at the time of confederation were faithfully carried out, but in 1912 when Hon. Frank Cochrane became Minister of Railways in the Borden government the rates on that railway were raised. As the rates were raised, and to the extent that they were raised, traffic was frozen along the Intercolonial railway; industries were forced out of business, and the raising of those rates contributed in a very large degree to the lamentable decline of industry in the maritime provinces which is so apparent at present. From 1918 to 1923 the Intercolonial railway was the only line in Canada which was not under the control of the Board of Railway Commissioners; various local rates were raised here and there and the shippers had no means of redress and no court to which they could appeal.
I am thoroughly in accord with the spirit and the provisions of this bill, and I wish to express the gratitude of a very great number of people in the maritime provinces for the step taken by the government in this matter. I deplore such remarks as that it is only a

The question then arises as to whether these reduced freight rates are going to solve the problem of the maritimes. Supposing this palliative which is now suggested by the government does not palliate; supposing it does not bring prosperity; what is going to be the consequence? Will the representatives of

the maritimes then come here, as has been suggested, and agitate for something more that they want, agitate to have the rate extended as far as Montreal, and if that does not help them sufficiently, to have it extended as far east as Toronto? Will there be any finality to it? The fact is, in my humble opinion, that reduced freight rates are not going to solve the problems of the maritime provinces, and I object to this legislation on the ground that it is going to give to the maritime provinces a preferential treatment which I do not think they ought to have any more than any other part of Canada. We are in this particular bill giving to a geographical area within the confines of confederation a preferential treatment, and in my opinion you cannot have confederation on a sound basis when you give preferential treatment to certain provinces within the confederation, because where you show favouritism on the one hand, you are bound to create an injustice on the other, and where you have an injustice you are going to have an agitation to have that injustice remedied. The consequence is we are now setting up a precedent for someone to come forward at a later date and ask for similar privileges for other parts of Canada. I am in favour of giving privileges to none, and of treating all people in all parts of Canada in exactly the same way.
It has been stated that the Crowsnest pass rates are in themselves something akin to what is proposed under this bill. Personally I cannot see the similarity at all. In the Crowsnest rates as existing at the present time a preference is given to a certain commodity which passes through three or four different provinces over a long haul. In this bill we are confining its provisions to the geographical area of three provinces, and we are giving a twenty per cent rebate on all local traffic in those provinces, in an area which commences and finishes in the three maritime provinces. It is altogether different from anything in the Crowsnest pass agreement as it exists at the present time, and those who try to show us that this is equal to or similar to the Crowsnest pass agreement are not, in my opinion, conversant with the situation.
I now come to the question as to how much this is going to help the great masses of people in Nova iScotia. Will it give the workers of Nova Scotia any better working conditions? Will it give them higher wages? I do not think so. I think that ultimately all the subsidies given under this bill will find their way to a very small percentage of the people of those provinces; the great masses of the people there will receive very

Canada during the period I have given with what the Intercolonial was able to accomplish during the same period in the maritime provinces.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I know the House is very anxious to adjourn by Easter, and I should not like to be held responsible for delaying prorogation, but I want to direct the attention of the Minister of Railways to the remarks made this afternoon by the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson). It seems to me that if this bill passes we are doing something very substantial for the maritime provinces. But the hon. member for York-Sunbury says the maritimes are not going to be satisfied until they get Montreal fixed as the western end of the Atlantic division of the Canadian National system. He also warns the government that this is only the first instalment of what the maritimes expect to get. If so, I am looking forward with a good deal of interest to what the " first instalment " is going to cost. Then maybe we can get some vague idea of the ultimate cost. The Postmaster General this afternoon referred to certain pledges made by Canada, or what was then Canada, to the maritime provinces to induce them to enter confederation, and he said that now we were only carrying out the terms that were really agreed to at that time. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that the provinces in western Canada had nothing whatever to do with any promise made to the maritimes, but I want to say right now that we do not object to any promises so made being carried out, although our only share in these to-day appears to be to help pay the bill. The railway commission found away back in 1914 that freight rates in western Canada were from 15 to 18 per cent higher than in the east. That view was concurred in by the late Hon. Frank Carvell in one of the judgments which he gave as chairman of the railway commission. It is true that the increases which have been made since that time were slightly larger in western Canada than in the east, but I think the railway commissioners themselves are still of the view that the rates in western Canada are higher in general than they are in the east. I cannot see how anyone can say that the maritimes are only getting justice if western Canada is called upon to pay her share of the 20 per cent which will probably have to be handed over by the government to the railways. If the maritimes consider that it is just that they should have lower freight rates than central Canada because central Canada gets some advantages from the tariff and other things, then I think that we in western Canada are justified in the statement that we are entitled to the same preferential treatment. Is the Minister
of Railways (Mr. Dunning) prepared to accept that as a principle in fixing freight rates in Canada to-day? The pledge I refer to, so far as I can find it in the report, is to the effect that the Intercolonial railway, having been built for strategic reasons and being therefore 200 miles or so longer than it would be if constructed in a direct line, should impose only such charges as would be justified in connection with a direct route. I do not think the maritimes are paying any greater charges to-day than they would if the line had been built over the shortest course; that is to say, the through rates to the maritimes are all based on the length of the Canadian Pacific Railway, short haul.
I would not object to the legislation now before us if it applied only to interprovincial traffic.^ If we wanted to do something to make it easier for the maritimes to trade with central Canada we should, in my opinion, give sympathetic consideration to such a proposal. But I do not see why one part of Canada should be singled out for preferential treatment in connection with local freight rates rather than any other section of the country. I do not see how the principle can be defended. I almost feel like saying that if the Minister of Railways can swallow that proposal, then surely we ought to admit that it is probable the whale did swallow Jonah.
I listened to the minister this afternoon as he spoke in support of this bill-or rather spoke on the bill, 'because I could not find very much in his speech that was in support of it. I may be doing him an injustice, and I do not want deliberately to do so. But, as nearly as I can remember, the reason he gave for bringing in this bill was that the Duncan commission had recommended it. I agree with the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) in the statement he made in his speech on the budget, that this investigation was a very one-sided affair, what the legal men, I believe, term an ex parte hearing. Only one side was represented. The Dominion government itself was too busy with an election campaign to be represented at the inquiry, and everybody else who should have been looking after this matter was also busy. But evidently somebody in the maritime provinces was interested and was busy entertaining the royal commission, putting them in the humour to recommend something that would certainly be [DOT] of some benefit to that part of Canada.

I want to ask: Since when has it been adopted as a principle, in the fixing of freight rates in Canada, that because operations in a particular part of the country are expensive, therefore there shall be a reduction there in freight rates? The people of Alberta and British Columbia particularly are suffering from high freight rates; the interprovincial rates, I believe, are 25 per cent above the level of the rates charged on the prairies. This is due to difficulty of railway operation on the Canadian Pacific between Alberta and British Columbia through the mountain section. Now, are we going to reverse our railway rate policy in Canada and declare that because of difficulties in the mountain section, similar to those referred to in the paragraph of the report I have just quoted, therefore lower freight rates will be conceded? The rates are higher on the prairies than they are in the maritime provinces at the present time, and I say without fear of contradiction that there is no part of Canada where railways can operate so cheaply as on the prairies, and particularly in the western end. They are not bothered much with snow and ice conditions there, although the general opinion in Canada may be very -much to the contrary. In the part of Alberta in which I live we never see a snow plow, and we have no snow and ice conditions to combat. Nevertheless we are paying higher rates.
It does seem to me that there is no true economic basis for this freight rate bill. I regret very much that a Liberal government has fallen for this idea of bonusing freight rates. Where is it going to stop? Why let us stop with the maritime provinces? Why have not the prairie provinces as much right to ask for the same thing? Why should) not the Peace River country ask for the same thing also; they are isolated a thousand miles away from the ocean? I would view the legislation very sympathetically, as I would view any legislation which would help bring western and eastern Canada closer together. May I say to hon. members that we in the west are under a great handicap. Under the tariff system of this country we are compelled1 to trade with central Canada; we are compelled to buy our supplies in central Canada; they must be hauled for a long distance across practically one thousand miles of rocks and Christmas trees, as one hon. member used to put it, and we have to pay the freight bill. Central Canada does not pay it; we pay the freight on everything we bring in and on everything we send out. Under these circumstances we feel, this long haul very keenly, and we sympathize with the maritime provinces in their endeavour to overcome a similar handicap. It is true that the haul in their case is not so long, but it presents a difficult problem. But we fail to understand, why local rates in the maritime provinces should be reduced 20 per cent with the Dominion government paying the bill, because that means that every section of Canada must pay a share. Because I think this policy is unsound, Mr. Speaker, I intend to vote against the second reading of the bill.

In regard to the difficulties of the maritime provinces in connection with freight rates, the increases in rates began, as has been said to-day, in 1913 when a 10 per cent increase was imposed on Intercolonial railway rates alone without any corresponding increase in rates in other parts of Canada. That was followed in July, 1915, by another increase of 5 per cent on Intercolonial rates, and still the rest of Canada suffered no increase. That was followed again in November, 1915, by another 5 per cent increase in rates on the Intercolonial railway alone. It was not until a year after that an increase of 5 per cent was made in freight rates in Canada, and I call the attention of the hon. member for Bow River to this fact that this first increase by the Board of Railway Commissioners applicable outside of the Intercolonial Railway applied only to stations east of Port Arthur. That was followed in 1948, March 15, by what is known as the 15 per cent increase which applied east and west both, but it excepted wheat, which is a pretty important commodity out west. That was followed again on August 32649-118
12, 1918, by a 25 per cent increase in rates all over Canada, but what happened? When that increase was imposed all over Canada, the 15 per cent increase which had been imposed by the previous order was knocked off so far as western Canada was concerned. That was followed on September 13, 1920, by a further 40 per cent increase-40 per cent in eastern Canada, and 35 per cent in western Canada. A provision was made that on January 1, 1921, a reduction was to take place, but the reduction in western Canada was a reduction down to 30 per cent of the previous rate, whereas the reduction in eastern Canada was a reduction down to 35 per cent of the previous rate. Thus, comparing eastern and western Canada respecting increases in freight rates, we have first a 10 per cent increase, then two 5 per cent increases and then a 15 per cent increase, all on eastern rates but not on western rates, and the first three of these applied to the Intercolonial railway alone.

I am going in a moment to deal with the argument that the decision of the commission was ex parte. They say:
The maritimes case on railway rates was put to us in very considerable detail. The railway *commission is at the present time dealing with *these same details, and we have not formed any opinion on these matters so far as a judgment [DOT]on their merits would involve consideration of railway administration and policy. On the broader question, however, of the incidence of the existing rates as a whole upon industry and employment in the maritimes, we have come very definitely to the conclusion that the rate .structure as it has been altered since 1912 has [DOT]placed upon the trade and commerce of the .maritime provinces (a) a burden which, as we have read the pronouncements and obligations undertaken at confederation-

With that as the starting point the commission proceed to say that in their judgment the changes which have been made in the rate structure since 1912, the increases which have taken place in the maritimes as compared with the rest of Canada, is as fair a measure as can be made of the disadvantages under which the three provinces suffered and of the special considerations which should be thought of when fixing the rate structure for those provinces.
They recommend a twenty per cent reduction in the local rates, Someone asks why. Let me deal with that for a moment. They recommend that the rates between stations on the Atlantic division shall be reduced by twenty per cent. I have already pointed out that that would only approximately put them back to the comparative position which they held before 1912, because there had been the various increases which had been made in the maritime rate structure, without corresponding increases in the rest of Canada. But there are reasons why the local rates in the maritime provinces should have been on a different basis, and might have been in the first place put and maintained on a different basis from the local rates in the rest of Canada. In the first place, the principle of rate-making is that the railways may charge "what the traffic will bear." That is the time honoured formula- not "all the traffic will bear," but "what it will bear." One factor is the value of the commodity. You naturally charge a higher rate on diamonds than on coal, and more per mile for a short haul where there is dense traffic than for a long haul where you have little traffic. These are all factors to be taken into consideration. Taking that as a basis the situation in the maritime provinces was that industries were from' time to time established for the benefit of the people of those provinces and for the manufacture of goods for domestic consumption. Rates were made on such a scale that the products of those industries would move to their customers. The position was not the same as in Ontario, where a man could manufacture goods and could almost throw them over his back fence into his customer's yard, but in the maritimes they had to move them a great many miles; therefore the unit rate had to be lower the further the goods had to travel. Another feature about the maritime traffic was that these goods were not canned in carload lots as they were in Upper Canada. Goods in the maritime provinces had to be moved as way freight

C.N.R.-Eastern Freight Rates
and consequently the class rate had to be lower than in Upper Canada where the same goods got the benefit of a low car load rate. Distributing centres gradually formed at Moncton, Sackville, Amherst, and other places. In all these places where wholesale houses were established, rates were fixed so that they could reach the local market and compete with the man from Ontario, who had the advantage of the through rate although they had a longer haul. These were some of the matters which entered into the rate making on the Intercolonial when it was a separate entity from the Canadian National Railways. And lastly, they were dealing with a population only one-fifth the density of Upper Canada; therefore if a man was to serve his customers and get his goods to market he had to have a lower rate, because he had less goods to handle, his average haul was longer, and he was unable to do business on the larger scale. And so because of these factors the local rates in 1912 were considerably lower than the rates in other parts of Canada.
Now in reference to the deficit, which has been so much talked about; notwithstanding the fact that the maritime provinces had 250 miles of non-commercial road, notwithstanding that they had as I say only one-fifth the density of population of the other provinces of Canada, that they had not the possibilities of trading enjoyed by other provinces, and the railroad had not the same traffic, the rates were such and the transportation tax imposed on the maritime provinces was such that in thirty-seven years there was only seven million dollars of a deficit on the Intercolonial. What would have happened if the 250 miles of railway had been cut out, and if we had been able to save our operating expenses on the 250 miles of road which was noncommercial? Take the lowest rate of operating expenses on any road in Canada and you will find that in ten years the maritime provinces would have saved, if that 250 miles of road were eliminated, some $14,000,000, which means that the deficit would have been wiped out and the maritime provinces would have shown a surplus. Hon. members must remember this fact-which was presented to the commission-that there are many other conditions in the maritimes which make it very expensive to operate the railroad, the climatic conditions, expensive terminals, car ferries-the effect of all these is included in the deficit.

That is the situation with regard to local rates. And so when the people of the maritime provinces discovered that the Intercolonial was being put in as part of the great National system and that all the rates were to be made uniform, they realized that difficulties would arise and that manufacturing and distributing centres which had flourished under the old conditions were likely to be adversely affected. As we all know, the situation did become worse. I am not one of those, Mr. Speaker, who contend that the only difficulty down in the maritime provinces is freight rates. I said that very frankly before the Board of Railway Commissioners a year ago, and I repeat it now; but I do feel that a return to the freight rate conditions which relatively speaking existed before 1912, will be of advantage to every producer and consumer in the maritime provinces. I am of course particularly interested in the fishing business of my constituency and while lower freight rates will be a benefit, the future of that great industry lies largely in the opening of wider markets, particularly in the United States. I cannot stress too strongly my personal opinion of the importance of continued and earnest activity with that object in view.
I am reminded that besides local rates there is another recommendation contained in this report and sought to be carried out by the bill. That recommendation is for a reduction of 20 per cent on the maritime or the Atlantic region proportion of the through rate. This simply means that the maritime manufacturer ought to be able to get his goods to Upper Canada on at least the same rate basis as if he distributed them locally. Montreal is the

speechtext: You will find in Ontario zones of two or three hundred miles where the rate is identical from any point within that zone to points outside. He will understand that the object of this bill is to get back by an arbitrary figure of 20 per cent reduction to the basis of 1912 when local rates were lower; or to put it another way,'to wipe out the disproportionate increases which have been made in maritime rates since 1912. His question is really why were the maritime rates lower before 1912?
I will try and restate what I have said, and

will put the last reason first. First, because of the sparse population; second, because of the long establishment of industrial centres in the maritimes, local rates from which were made sufficiently low to enable manufactured products to move to the manufacturer's customers; third, because of the establishment of distributing centres at certain points in the maritimes and the fixing of distributing rates to move the goods, and, fourth, because of the small volume of goods moved, the less than carload rates had to be made considerably lower than in Ontario and other parts of Canada where goods generally speaking moved at the low carload rate.

The peculiar thing was that after the rates were raised in the maritimes in 1918 and 1919 on the amalgamation of the Intercolonial with the larger system the deficits began to increase, and instead of one or two million dollars they were from five to six million dollars a year although the rates were higher.

C.N.R.-Eastern Freight Rates
The lower westbound rate permits the maritime manufacturer to deal with his customers in upper 'Canada and to compete with Ontario and Quebec firms. I wish to put on record what I think is of some significance in our national development. I confess it was a surprise to me when it took place at the meeting of the Board of Railway Commissioners in Moncton. Quite unsolicited, a resolution was presented from the Board of Trade of Toronto formally and distinctly recognizing that the maritime provinces were entitled to a market in Quebec and upper Canada. The last paragraph is, I think, worthy of going on Hansard. It was read by Mr. Thomas Marshall, traffic manager of the Toronto Board of Trade, and is as follows:
The Toronto Board of Trade is desirous that our friends of the maritime provinces obtain some measure of relief which will assist them in marketing their products in the central provinces, and to that end would favour extending to them a reasonable westbound freight rate differential, and feel that in so far as the membership of this. board of trade is concerned it would not object to such an adjustment in class rates as would be found necessary to recoup the carriers for loss in revenue ensuing from such a reduction in the westbound rates.
It pretty nearly marks an epoch in the history of the Dominion when a board of trade in central Canada says, in effect, if the railways are going to lose by making a rate which permits the maritime shipper to send his goods to the markets of Ontario and Quebec, we are willing that there shall be such an adjustment as will recoup the carriers for that loss. I thought it showed a very fine spirit. Somebody will ask, why are not east-bound rates reduced also? For a very good reason, well known, they tell me, in freight rate making. The man on the circumference who has to trade towards the centre is entitled to a little better rate than the man who, situated in the centre, can trade towards both sides of the circle. Therefore, while the Halifax or St. John shipper gets a certain rate to Montreal or Toronto, the Toronto man will not, under the recommendations of the Duncan report, receive equal consideration coming east. The rate which will take goods from Halifax to Toronto will probably bring goods from Toronto only as far as Truro; or, putting it the other way, the rate for goods from Toronto to Halifax will probably carry goods from Halifax to a point, 100 miles west of Toronto. As I say, the man on the seaboard can trade only in one direction and he is therefore entitled to an advantage. Some people have been shocked by this, but I may assure the House that this provision was recognized in the freight rates as they
existed up to 1912. For example, the rate from Montreal to Halifax was 56 cents, whereas from Halifax to Montreal it was only 50 cents. In May 1912, however, the whole thing was ironed out, and a 56 cent rate was inaugurated both ways. Before 1912 from Montreal to Sydney the rate was 64 cents as against a rate from Sydney to Montreal of 55 cents. The same thing appertains in th<3 United States. The rate from Chicago to Boston is SI.49 per 100 first class, whereas from Boston to Chicago it is only $1.42; from St. Louis to Boston it is $1.73, and from Boston to St. Louis, $1.66. The difference was specially accentuated on what we know as the differential all-rail route, which is a route in the United States from Boston to Chicago participated in to a large extent by Canadian lines, and the differential there is as great as. on the standard all-rail route. The through rate from Chicago to Boston is $1.49 whereas from Boston to Chicago it is $1.42 the reason for the lower rate in one direction being as I have stated.
I will not at this stage deal at any length with the question of international rates, but in committee I shall if necessary have a word or two to say with regard to the international and import rates which are excluded from the provisions of this bill. I do not want to delay the House further with any citation of rates. I merely want to emphasize what I stated a few moments ago with reference to my appreciation of the provisions of this bill and the manner in which the Duncan report has been received. The bill will, I think, be found to be a practical implementing of the Duncan report, as to local and through Canadian rates. But it is something more than that. There are in the maritime provinces certain roads which are not under the control of the Canadian National Railways; I might mention the Dominion Atlantic railway, owned by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, the Canadian Pacific from St. John to Montreal, the Sydney and Louisburg, the Cumberland Railway and Coal Company's road from Springhill to Parrsboro, and some others. These are not dealt with directly by the Duncan report, but the commission suggests that if, as the result of a reduction of rates on the Canadian National Railways, the "other great railway system" meaning of course the Canadian Pacific Railway, finds itself prejudiced, then "equitable consideration" should be given it. This means that if, in the case of the Dominion Atlantic Railway for example, the conditions were such that it was competing with the Canadian National Railways on some certain traffic and had to bring its rates down to

the new reduced rate of the Canadian National in order to hold the business, then the government should make some provision to help out. But there is no suggestion anywhere in the report that if the Dominion Atlantic is not forced by competition to reduce its rates, the government shall come to the assistance of those making use of the railway. [DOT]In other words the report only applies in terms to traffic on the Canadian National Railways or on such portions of the Canadian Pacific as are in direct competition and therefore have to reduce their rates. Section 9 of the bill provides however that all railways in the maritime provinces, whether competitive or otherwise, who reduce their rates below the normal in accordance with the spirit of the act, shall be reimbursed. It seems to me that this is carrying out in a broad spirit and not in the spirit of the half loaf, as suggested by one hon. gentleman opposite this afternoon, the recommendations submitted in the Duncan report. It meets the practical situation more than half-way, for it shows a determination to do full justice by the people of the maritime provinces and is an evidence that the government, having put its hand to the plough, will not turn back and that the shipper on a line other than the Canadian National has not been forgotten. By the way it has been said that the Dominion was not represented on the hearings before the commission. That is true, but the railways and their experts and their counsel were there, and it must be remembered also that the very constitution of the tribunal was such as to justify confidence in the thoroughness of its investigation and to ensure that all statements made and contentions put forward were duly tested and weighed.
I am not standing here as a special pleader for the maritime provinces. While it is true I come from Nova Scotia, I fully realize my responsibilities as a member of the government of Canada. Let me remind the House that confederation was, in the broad sense of the term, a partnership entered into by four provinces. Five more have come in and there is no use ini our trying to get along if some of the provinces are unhappy and discontented. I believe that a reasonable effort has been made to bring contentment where there has been dissatisfaction. We in the maritime provinces have had no quarrel with the rest of Canada in anything that this Dominion has done to benefit other sections of the country. When other provinces have received what they felt to be their due, in order that their prosperity as members of Canadian confederation might be assured, we have always ungrudgingly supported their

claims. When the province of Quebec added to her domain what was virtually an empire, when her railways were subsidized, her canals deepened, and Montreal was made an ocean port; when Ontario had her area trebled and her canals built; when Manitoba was doubled in area and means were afforded whereby the products of that province could be marketed at a cost 25 per cent lower than could the products of the country immediately to the south; when Alberta and Saskatchewan, in view of special circumstances, received substantial annual subsidies to facilitate their entry into the Dominion in at least comparative affluence; when, in the interests of British Columbia the construction of three transcontinental railways was authorized and that province had extended to her certain special treatment in relation to her railways; when all these benefits were received by the other provinces of Canada the people of the maritimes gladly acknowledged the right of their fellow citizens to generous treatment. It is in the same spirit of justice that the maritime provinces appeal to the House to-day to recognize the claims now made and to support the legislation now being brought down implementing the recommendations of the Duncan commission. My hon. friends in the far corner opposite suggest that railway rates are not the only thing. I agree and they seem to have overlooked that the program announced by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) on March 25 included a great deal more than freight rates.
I want to impress upon the House that this report and this legislation mean much more to the people of the maritime provinces than is involved in a mere mathematical calculation, or in the printed words of a statute. I believe it will be and in fact it has already been received by the people of my native province as an earnest and genuine evidence of the practical good-will which those in other parts of the Dominion bear toward them. And so the people of these provinces will I believe realize that their fellow citizens throughout the country have sympathy with them-and in using that word sympathy, I mean it in its root sense as "thinking along with" them-and when you get different races, different provinces or different localities thinking along with one another there cannot be much doubt of their ultimate understanding and of the agreement and unity which is bound to follow. We have industry and energy and intelligence down there by the sea. Our people have become a bit discouraged, sometimes irritable, and, most disturbing of all, have felt a sense of injustice. I am prepared to believe, how-

ever, as I want the House to believe, that this legislation brings to them a new outlook, a new conception of Canadian unity, a new determination to ply their individual trades and vocations with vigour and industry and thrift, and a renewed eagerness to help make this Dominion, as a whole and without distinction as to provincial boundaries, a better place in which to live and a model of contentment and progress for the democracies of the world.

Mr. Speaker, I a.m sure the
whole House enjoyed the very able exposition of conditions in the maritime provinces which has just fallen from the lips of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston). It must be remembered', however, that the bill with which we have been dealing this afternoon is a concrete proposal. The debate on the second reading of this bill has assumed rather wide proportions, and 'has involved a discussion of practically the whole maritime situation and a very general discussion of the Duncan report itself. In the few remarks which I propose to offer this evening I will try to confine myself to the bill now before us, which is entitled, "An act respecting the Canadian National railways and the tariffs of tolls to be charged on certain eastern lines." Lest silence on tihe part of those sitting to your left, Mr. Speaker, should be construed as dissent from the proposal, I desire to offer a few remarks.
We on this side of the House desire in every way to facilitate the passage of these proposals arising out of the Duncan report, and desire likewise to expedite the passage of the various measures. The report has been before parliament and the country for several months now, and we assume that we have all read it, considered it and digested it. Personally I can say I have considered it very fully; I have discussed it with many men qualified to speak upon the subject and have also discussed it from an academic point of view in one of our institutions of learning. Therefore I have no hesitation in saying, Mr. Speaker, that as far as it goes the Duncan report is acceptable to those who constitute the official opposition in this chamber.
It is not my intention to go over the whole question to-night; I think it is unnecessary, and I will content myself with this remark; This is the second reading of a bill, but throughout the whole afternoon and evening it has resembled very much the discussion of a bill in committee. I have no objection to that if we do not have to go through the same discussion when the bill gets into committee, but I do think it has gone pretty far for a discussion on the second reading of a bill such as this. I am satisfied from a careful study of this bill that it carries out the main features of the Duncan report in regard to freight rates, and as such it should be adopted by this House. I do not consider and have never considered the maritime provinces in the position of communities basing their claims upon charitable grounds; I have always considered the claims advanced by these provinces to be founded upon principles of equity and justice, and the more I have studied them the less reason I find to dissent from any of the views expressed by Sir Andrew Rae Duncan and his colleagues in this report. If I could offer a criticism it would be that the report does not perhaps go far enough in the way of remedial arrangements for the maritime provinces. I agree with the argument of 'the Minister of National Defence; I could enlarge upon it very much, perhaps, but I am satisfied that the House is now fully seized of the whole situation, and under the circumstances I believe it is our duty to pass these bills as expeditiously as possible.

Mr. Speaker. I may say that I have no intention of being intimidated by those cries of "question"; I intend to say what I have to say and if there are any interruptions it will mean that I will accupy the time of the House so much longer.
At the outset may I say that I wish to make a few observations on this bill, and in doing so I find myself in the somewhat unhappy position of differing with the rest of my colleagues in this part of the House, differing not on principle but on practice, not on fundamentals so much as on incidentals. I feel, Sir, that in the consideration of maritime problems I must defer, and I think we from the west must defer, to a considerable extent at least to those gentlemen from that section of the country who should understand better than we from the far west can understand what their particular section of the country requires. In tihe last few years we have had under consideration many western problems, and in the consideration of those problems the members from the maritime .provinces, from Ontario, Quebec and British Columbia were obliged of necessity to defer to us, who understood those problems and who should know the ibest remedies. Nevertheless, Sir, it is fitting and proper that I should give my own opinions of the problems of the maritime provinces, and in
C.N.R.-Eastern Freight Rales

so doing I do not wish to express myself dogmatically at all; I am not inferring that they are really the problems of the maritimes, because I am prepared to leave' that largely to the members from that section of the country. I wish to give to the House, however, what I feel to be some of the problems of the maritimes which have not been dealt with in this report.
May I say, first, that as I understand it the lack of markets is perhaps one of the fundamental problems facing the maritime provinces to-day, and in a measure at least that may be due to the protective system under which this country has been run for many years. Perhaps I may be pardoned if I have a little more sympathy for that part of the country than some of my friends who have never lived there, because half of my life was spent in the provinces by the sea. I well recall in my boyhood days hearing many bitter acrimonious debates on the question of the protective system, and I recall that in Prince Edward Island at any rate in the early days the great majority of the people were of the opinion that they had lost something by entering confederation, that by coming under the Canadian protective tariff they had lost the markets of the United States which they considered they could have held if they' had remained out of confederation. I am not going to state whether or not that is so; I am simply going to give the House the impressions I received in my boyhood days when I heard these questions discussed in that part of the country.
I remember the feeling in the maritimes in 1896, when the Liberal party came into power after being out of office for many years; the great mass of the people thought the promises of Sir Wilfrid Laurier and Sir Richard Cartwright would be put into effect immediately, and a good many people thought that on the day after the election the grass would grow greener than it had been the day before, that the wheels of industry would start to hum in the maritimes and that the thousands of their young men and young women who had sought jobs and made homes in the United States would in time come back to the maritimes. But, Sir, they were disappointed. I am not going to enter into the history of that time, but the fact was that the new government simply carried on the policies of the old. They usurped the Conservative policy and no change whatever in tariff policy followed the change in government. It is possible that the maritimes sacrificed something in coming into confederation. It is possible that if they were outside

of confederation to-day, they might negotiate with the United States a reciprocity treaty which would be of some advantage to them and, by admitting United States manufactured goods in free or at reduced rates of duty, they might be able to secure a favourable position for trade in that part of the country. I am not prepared to take a dogmatic stand on that. That may or may not be so. But I feel that those provinces sacrificed something in this regard when they entered confederation, and because they sacrificed something, it behooves the Canadian parliament to reimburse them, in a measure at least, for what they have lost.
I agree with the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Gardiner) that, in so far as I have studied the question, the troubles of the maritimes are due in some degree to the centralization of banking power, the centralization of the control of our banks. Some hon. gentlemen from the maritimes in this chamber to-night seemed to question the opinion of the hon. member for Acadia when he made a similar statement on the floor of this House. But I have in my hand a pamphlet written by the Hon. F. B. McCurdy, who is not unknown to many of my hon. friends, and he places this as one of the principal problems of the maritime provinces.

I bow to your ruling. I submit however that the preamble should give me the right to discuss anything dealt with by the Duncan report. In conclusion on this point I will read the closing sentence in this pamphlet. He says:
Centralization and autocratic control are rampant in this country, as well as the States, and it is not improbable that the next revolt in that great country will be against the system that is rapidly reducing the human being to the position of an inarticulate cog in a huge machine that operates for profit alone.
I wish to deal briefly with the reference made by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) to the Crowsnest pass rates, and in this at least, I assume that I am in order because I am discussing the question of freight rates. The minister stated that those rates were not profitable to the railways. I think he quoted Mr. Watson of the Canadian National Railways as stating that in 1926 the haulage of grain in western Canada meant a loss of $6,000,000 to the Canadian
National Railways. I will give my hon. friend in that regard a few figures which will perhaps convince him and which, I think, should convince any reasonably minded member that the Crowsnest pass rates to-day are profitable to both of the great railway systems.
First, I might refer to the freight rate investigation in 1922 before a committee of this House. Before that committee we find Mr. Beatty, president of the Canadian Pacific railway, predicting that if the Crowsnest pass rates came into effect in the next year, the Canadian Pacific railway would fall short by $15,000,000 of paying its fixed charges and dividends. That is a remarkable statement. Yet what do we find? In addition to paying fixed charges and dividends we find that the Canadian Pacific had a larger surplus than they had the previous year. That was after the Crowsnest pass rates had been in operation for one year, so we see how much the predictions of these officials are to be relied upon when the question is one of dollars and cents to them and when they are trying to influence a committee of this House.
I am not going to weary the House with lengthy quotations, but we find Mr. Hanna, president of the Canadian National Railways, making similar predictions for that road. He predicted that the deficit in 1922 would be $26,000,000 or $10,000,000 more than it was in 1921. Instead of that the deficit was considerably less than it was the previous year. I am going to give just a few figures for different months which, I think, should show clearly to any unbiased mind that the handling of grain means a considerable profit to both the railway systems. I will take the Canadian Pacific Railway for the year 1924. For the first four months of that year their net earnings were a little over $5,000,000. For the next four months, May, June, July and August, their net earnings amounted to $9,000,000. Those were the eight months in which little or no grain was being moved. When we come to the next period, September, October, November and December, the four months in which the great bulk of the traffic is grain, what do we find? We find that instead of $5,000,000 or $9,000,000, the net earnings amounted to $22,000,000 or more than for the previous eight months.
In the first four months of 1925 the net earnings amounted to $4,980000; in the next four months they amounted to $10,000,000; but in the last four months of the year, the months in which again the great bulk of the grain was handled, we find the net earnings increased to the enormous total of $26,500,000. Surely in face of those figures

C.K.R.-Eastern Freight Rates
no hon. gentleman who will give intelligent consideration to the subject can say that grain is being transported at a loss. Again we find that in the year 1925 the net profit was $23,000,000, but the four grain-handling months accounted for over $20,000,000 of that $23,000,000. I have similar figures here for the Canadian National Railway. I find that in 1924 their total net revenue was $11,764,000, of which $11,197,000, or almost the whole thing, was earned in the four months in which the grain was being moved.
When we come to the operating ratio, which is really one of the decisive indications, telling us how much money the railway has to spend to earn a dollar, I find that in 1921 the operating ratio of the Canadian Pacific Railway was 82.28; that is, the railway had to spend 82.28 cents to earn one dollar. The next year, 1922, was the year in which the Crowsnest rates were fully in effect, the year in which Mr. Beatty predicted that their net earnings would fall below the amount necessary to pay fixed charges and dividends, but what do we find? Instead of increasing, we find that the operating ratio decreased to 80.55; in other words, the railway made 2 per cent more profit than the year before, and so on; the profits crawled up year after year. That should clearly prove to anyone that the Crowsnest rates mean a profit to both railway systems.
In the consideration of the particular question before the House I must admit that I cannot find room for the criticism of the government that has come from other speakers in this section of the House. I am not entirely convinced that this is the fundamental remedy. I believe that there are probably other remedies. I think there are other questions that the Duncan commission might have investigated and should have reported on. But looking at it from the strictly legal point of view and from the standpoint of precedent, which is what seems to govern everything in this House, the government appointed a commission to inquire into the grievances, alleged or real, of the maritime provinces. They appointed a commission of able, capable men. I think this House would have approved of the personnel of the commission had it been asked to do so. The commission came back and made a very definite report to the government, and for the life of me I can hardly see what else could be expected of the government than to carry out these recommendations. Therefore I find myself in the position where I cannot criticize the government for carrying out the report of their own commission. The bill we are considering was

framed with that end in view, to carry out the recommendations of the commission.
When I listened to the speeches of several of my colleagues in this section of the House, I compared them with speeches I heard here in 1922 against the Crowsnest rates, when some of the members from the maritime provinces opposed, and bitterly opposed that legislation, and again in 1924 they opposed the building of the Hudson Bay railway and many other issues of interest to the west. I think, after all, we have to be a little broader. We have, as Bums would say, to try and see ourselves as others see us. We have to try and judge a thing from the other fellow's standpoint. I believe the members from the maritime provinces who opposed the construction of the Hudson Bay railway, and who very bitterly criticised the decision of parliament in 1922 to reinstate the Crowsnest rates, were just as honest and sincere in opposing those measures as my friends in this comer of the House are in opposing this. They looked at it from the standpoint of the maritime provinces. They were not as well acquainted with the problems of the west as we were. But in the last analysis parliament deferred to the wishes of the west, and I think in this matter we have at least to defer to the wishes and opinions of the people of the maritime provinces.
The question of rural credits, for instance, is not one of interest to the people of the maritime provinces. When I visit down there the people I meet always want to know why we in the west should want the parliament of Canada to give us cheap money. They say they can alwa]^ go to a neighbour and borrow what they want at five per cent. They do not understand our problem, and naturally they object to parliament, for which they have a responsibility, being tied up to this thing. Another thing I always hear about when I visit down in the maritime provinces is the Crowsnest rates. The people there seem to think they have a distinct grievance on that account. Some people whom I know will always be convinced that parliament did them a great injustice in 1922, when it gave us a rate which they think is not profitable to the railwa]''. Again, take a measure such as the amendment to the Canada Grain Act, which is of vital importance to western Canada. Our maritime friends offered no objection to those amendments, although most of them are not interested in the matter, and a good many of them may think that it is not striking at the root of our problems in the west, but they were fair and deferred to our judgment in the matter because we were dealing with our own

C.N.U.-Eastern Freight Rales
problems, and I am asking my hon. friends in this part of the House to grant to the people of the maritime provinces the same consideration which we have received at tiheir hands in these other matters.
Another great burning question in western Canada to-day is the return of our natural resources, and just here I might say that it is a matter of concern to our people to see something extra new being given to the maritime provinces when we see by this report that a province like New Brunswick is securing 375 per cent of its revenue from its forests; when we do not even control our own timber. That is a grievance of ours, but I realize that to oppose the granting of this measure of relief to the maritime provinces will not assist us in western Canada to get possession of our natural resources. I ask my hon. friends from the maritime provinces to continue to extend to us the consideration which they have in the past, and at some future time I trust that this parliament will be fair to us and give back to us our natural resources, which are of vital importance to us.

Our railways wanted the reduction continued. The United States lines however, flatly refused to continue the reduced) rates, although they agreed to one month's extension into 1926. The other lines involved cover such a wide range of types of railway operation that it was difficult to arrive at a suitable wording. I may say that in one draft I had the word "shall", and found, in connection with some of the local lines, that they had special freight tariffs of their own higher than the rates now in effect in the area referred to and especially authorized by the railway commission as a result of particular conditions operating in that area. Therefore I thought it advisable to leave the matter permissive instead of mandatory. My hon. friend is probably interested and I know the hon. member for Hants-Kings (Mr. Ilsley) is interested in whether or not the Dominion Atlantic Railway, which, while a separate corporation, is owned by the Canadian Pacific and which serves a large portion of Nova Seotia, will put these reductions into effect. I may say in that connection that, as soon as the financial resolution appeared on the order paper, the Canadian Pacific very naturally wanted to know where they came in. As a result of interviews and consultations between the parties affected, including some of the other railways as well as the Canadian Pacific, the present clause as it appears in the reprinted bill was evolved. During those consultations I received from President Beatty of the Canadian Pacific absolute assurance that these rates would be met in full on all lines controlled by the Canadian Pacific in the area affected. Further than that I cannot go.
With respect to other lines of railway I am finding new lines of railway down in the mari-times every day or two. I get a wire from some railway 1 never heard of before and which I find some of my maritime friends never heard of before asking if they will not be permitted to put this tariff into force and to secure the benefits of clause 9 in the reprinted bill. I feel sure that this feature of the clause will work out satisfactorily without being mandatory, because if it were mandatory, other more serious problems would arise in connection with some of the local lines.

subtopic: FREIGHT RATES TO BE CHARGED ON EASTERN LINES
speechtext:
Are we to understand that
this clause covers practically all railways in the maritimes outside of the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific? I am very much interested in the Dominion Atlantic Railway because it runs through the whole of my constituency. It is one of the prominent railways in Nova Scotia; it covers 217 miles from Yarmouth to Halifax, one of the most important parts of the province. I want to know distinctly from the minister whether it is going to 'be included in this 20 per cent reduction.

subtopic: FREIGHT RATES TO BE CHARGED ON EASTERN LINES
speechtext: As I said a few moments ago the Dominion Atlantic, if it so desires, may under clause 9 file a tariff meeting the tariff set forth in this legislation. I have the assurance of President Beatty of the Canadian Pacific, which controls the Dominion Atlantic, that such tariffs will be filed and that the rates will be met on the Dominion Atlantic.	[DOT]

subtopic: FREIGHT RATES TO BE CHARGED ON EASTERN LINES
speechtext: I take it that under this particular clause the country will be called upon to reimburse to railways other than the Canadian National the full 20 per cent reduction.

subtopic: FREIGHT RATES TO BE CHARGED ON EASTERN LINES
speechtext:
Again I can only refer my hon. friend to the language of the clause. It was a very difficult thing to devise because of the fact that, if we said in so many words that the difference between existing normal rates and the rates reduced by 20 per cent would for all time, or at least so long as this statute remained in existence, be paid by the Dominion, we might very well run into difficulty in a few years time on account of increases in the volume of traffic consequent upon the reduction and a consequent decrease in operating ratio due to a greater density of traffic, while the Dominion would still be paying the flat 20 per cent. In drafting this clause an effort has been made to get around the difficulty by providing that the railway commission shall be required to certify what would have been the normal tolls on that railway in that area if this special legislation had not been in effect. In that way we hope to have the conditions sufficiently elastic so that if there is a great increase in traffic and, as a consequence of greater density, a better operating ratio is obtained, the Dominion government will not then be compelled to pay the full 20 per cent. That is the principle of section 9. But my hon. friend is quite correct, that to start with 20 per cent will have to be borne by the government.
I Mr. Dunning.]

subtopic: FREIGHT RATES TO BE CHARGED ON EASTERN LINES
speechtext: Otherwise it will be put up to the railway commission to say whether lower rates will be charged?

subtopic: FREIGHT RATES TO BE CHARGED ON EASTERN LINES
speechtext:
No. If my hon. friend will read subsection 3 he will see that it provides:
The board on approving any tariff under this section shall certify the normal tolls which but for this act would have been effective and shall, in the case of each company, at the end of each calendar year promptly ascertain and certify to the Minister of Railways and Canals the amount of the difference between the tariff tolls and the normal tolls above referred to on all traffic moved by the company during such year under the tariff so approved.
If my hon. friend will then read subsection 4, he will see that it provides:
The board shall, in every third year and at any time upon the request of the governor in council, ascertain and certify to the Minister of Railways and Canals whether under the provisions of the Railway Act, the normal tolls referred to in subsection three hereof, should be revised and in the event of such revision the revised normal tolls shall thereafter be used instead of the normal tolls referred to in the said subsection in calculating the difference to be paid to the company thereunder.

subtopic: FREIGHT RATES TO BE CHARGED ON EASTERN LINES
speechtext: Suppose that through the reduction the traffic increases considerably so that in 1928 the railway companies will .make more money than they made in 1926; would the government still have to pay this 20 per cent?

subtopic: FREIGHT RATES TO BE CHARGED ON EASTERN LINES
speechtext: I expect that it will be the duty of the Department of Railways and Canals each year to watch the operation of this statute with great care. In each third year it will be the duty of the railway commission in any case to take into account such factors as that mentioned by my hon. friend, but in addition to that being done every third year, the governor in council may demand that it be done at any time in order to ensure that there shall be a reasonable parity between the improvement made in operating ratio upon the railway and the amount paid annually by the Dominion.

subtopic: FREIGHT RATES TO BE CHARGED ON EASTERN LINES
speechtext: Does the $2,500,000 which the minister mentioned a moment ago include all that we shall have to pay next year under the 20 ,per cent reduction?

subtopic: FREIGHT RATES TO BE CHARGED ON EASTERN LINES
speechtext:
We propose to celebrate the diamond jubilee of confederation by bringing this act into effect on July 1st, so the whole year will not be involved. But on the basis of the 1926 volume of business and on the basis of the spread set out in this law, it will be about $2,500,000 a year; that is to say, if it runs from the 1st of July, 1927, to the 1st of July, 1928, I would estimate that about $2,500,000 may be involved.

subtopic: FREIGHT RATES TO BE CHARGED ON EASTERN LINES
speechtext: And as the traffic improves, the spread diminishes; is that right?

subtopic: FREIGHT RATES TO BE CHARGED ON EASTERN LINES
speechtext: We hope it will.

subtopic: FREIGHT RATES TO BE CHARGED ON EASTERN LINES
speechtext: Some time ago I asked a question as to that part of the Canadian Pacific railway line which runs through the state of Maine, and the minister said he would give an explanation on section 9.

subtopic: FREIGHT RATES TO BE CHARGED ON EASTERN LINES
speechtext:
Subsection 1 of section 9 speaks for itself. It says:
(1) Other companies owning or operating lines of railway in or extending into the select territory may file with the board tariffs of tolls respecting freight movements similar to the preferred movements, meeting the statutory rates referred to in section seven of this act.
That means that the Canadian National Railway under this act has a certain rate from Halifax to Montreal; that is the outbound movement referred to in a previous section. The Canadian Pacific also has an outbound rate from Halifax to Montreal. The fact that the Canadian Pacific passes through the state of Maine makes no difference whatever. They meet the Canadian National rate between these two points, and hence they get the benefit on that portion of the mileage which is in the maritime provinces.

speechtext:
Do they get the 20 per cent on that portion which is not in the maritime
provinces?

subtopic: FREIGHT RATES TO BE CHARGED ON EASTERN LINES
speechtext:
The railway commission
will certify what the tariff would have been but for the existence of this legislation, and they will be paid that.

subtopic: FREIGHT RATES TO BE CHARGED ON EASTERN LINES
speechtext: I would ask the minister to be good enough to explain to me just what is meant in the fourth line of subsection 4, where it says: "whether under the provisions of the Railway Act, the normal tolls referred to in subsection 3 hereof, should be revised."

subtopic: FREIGHT RATES TO BE CHARGED ON EASTERN LINES
speechtext: The normal tolls are the tolls at present in existence on the lines in question and approved by the board-the tolls which would continue to be in existence but for this act-the tolls which necessarily must be used as the basis of calculation for the payment to be made to railways other than the Canadian National. My hon. friend will see therefore in a moment the importance of having the ordinary provisions of the Railway Act apply to a revision of these normal tolls, although they are no longer being used for freight rate purposes, but merely for the purpose of calculating what is due the railways under the statute. Therefore we require to have provision made whereby the railway commission can revise the tolls which should have been charged but for this legislation. Is that clear to my hon. friend?

subtopic: FREIGHT RATES TO BE CHARGED ON EASTERN LINES
speechtext:
I would ask this question to clarify it:	Does this subsection mean that
if the rates outside of the maritime provinces should go up or down, a change will be made in the 20 per cent such as to keep the rates in the maritime provinces at the level they will be under this act when it comes into force?

subtopic: FREIGHT RATES TO BE CHARGED ON EASTERN LINES
speechtext: I cannot follow my hon. friend there; I do not quite know where he is going. But perhaps he would be satisfied with this general assurance, that all the provisions for elasticity under the control of the railway commission which could be inserted in this act have been inserted.
